Infection begins when the viral Gn protein docks onto host surface receptors, using integrin and protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) (Gavrilovskaya et al., 1999; Jangra et al., 2018). Once internalized via endocytosis, a drop in endosomal pH forces the viral envelope to fuse with the host membrane, releasing the genome into the cytoplasm. The viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) starts both transcription and genome replication, before structural proteins and newly synthesized RNA assemble at the Golgi complex or plasma membrane prior to budding out as mature infectious virions (see Figure 1) (Hussein et al., 2011; Hepojoki et al., 2012; Vaheri et al., 2013b; Bradfute et al., 2024). Current orthohantavirus management relies on supportive care and repurposed drugs with limited efficacy. To overcome this public health issue, this review presents existing treatment strategies and advocates for modern in silico approaches like molecular docking. Specifically, we highlight the potential of rational drug design, encouraging the systematic virtual screening of diverse chemical and natural product libraries to discover accessible, broad-spectrum hantaviral treatments. Viral entry and fusion inhibitors One of the most promising strategies to inhibit hantaviral entry into host cells is the use of cyclic peptides. With the help of a phage library, where peptide libraries are displayed on the surfaces of filamentous bacteriophages, Larson et al. (2005) identified cyclic nonapeptides that bind the b3-integrin receptor, which pathogenic orthohantaviruses like Sin Nombre virus (SNV), Hantaan virus (HTNV), Seoul virus (SEOV), and Puumala virus (PUUV) bind for viral entry into human endothelial cells. Key stages of cellular infections are shown. Red crosses (X) indicate specific steps targeted by the therapeutic interventions discussed in the review. Adapted from Jonsson et al. (2010); Mir (2010); Vaheri et al. This peptide was further refined to its minimal functional unit required through alanine substitution and deletion scanning to the cyclic pentapeptide cyclo-[CPFVC] (Hall et al., 2007). However, because free monovalent peptides were less effec- tive than those presented on phage, subsequent research (Hall et al., 2008) shifted towards presenting peptides in a multivalent format on nanoparticles and targeting the orthohantavirus glycoproteins directly rather than the host b3-integrin receptor. The three most potent binders of the virion were selected and attached to 100 nm nanoparticles to create a multivalent inhibitor. When the peptide CLVRNLAWC was presented on a nanoparticle at a 4:1 ratio, its inhibition of SNV jumped from 9% (as a free peptide) to 32.5%. However, the peptide CQATTARNC achieved an even higher efficacy, with inhibition surpassing 50% when the nanoparticle- to-virus ratio was increased to 20:1 (Hall et al., 2008). Building on these strategies, the research was expanded to Andes virus (ANDV). Using a similar approach, Hall et al. (2009) eluted the peptide library from purified ANDV particles using monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) against the Gn and Gc glycoproteins. A major finding in this study was the combined use of peptides that targeted different Gn- and Gc-specific sequences resulted in synergistic inhibition (anti-Gc/Gn peptides CMQSAAAHC and CTVGPTRSC) of infec- tion that was significantly more powerful than single-peptide treatments, emphasizing the benefit of targeting multiple viral epitopes (Hall et al., 2009). Lastly, to search for peptidomimetic molecules to block SNV infection, Hall et al. (2010) used the 3D structure of the previously refined pentapeptide cyclo-[CPFVC], in a ligand-based virtual screening approach to evaluate over 600,000 small molecules. This transition from biological peptides to drug- like peptidomimetics identified compounds such as G319–0078 and 8012-0652, which were 2,000 times more potent than the original cyclic peptides. These molecules demonstrated high-affinity inhibi- tion in the nanomolar range in vitro (EC50 values between 1.3 - 2.5 nM) (Hall et al., 2010), successfully evolving the initial lead into a highly potent preclinical candidate warranting further in vivo evaluation. Another distinct strategy to prevent infection focuses on dis- rupting the viral membrane fusion process. Because the orthohantavirus Gc glycoprotein functions as a class II fusion protein, completing membrane fusion requires a major structural relocation of Domain III (DIII) to achieve the post-fusion state (Barriga et al., 2016; Arata-Salas et al., 2026). Exploiting this mechanical vulnerability, Barriga et al. (2016) demonstrated that viral entry can be successfully blocked using recombinant fragments and synthetic peptides derived from the Gc DIII and stem region. These fragments allow initial Gc trimerization to proceed but ultimately inhibit the pathway by preventing membrane hemifusion and fusion pore formation (Barriga et al., 2016). The recombinant DIII fragment inhibited ANDV fusion by around 70% at 25 μM and demonstrated cross-reactivity by reducing PUUV-mediated fusion by 50%. Even greater potency was observed with the R2 peptide, derived from the C-terminal part of the Gc stem region, which inhibited ANDV fusion by up to 95% in vitro (Barriga et al., 2016). Although efficacy dropped to a 70% cross-reduction (at 20 μM) against PUUV-mediated fusion (Barriga et al., 2016) due to its high genetic divergence between the two viruses, it still demonstrates significant cross-protective potential. Another very potent cell-entry inhibitor is Griffithsin (GRFT), an algae-derived lectin that has demonstrated high efficacy against several enveloped viruses such as coronaviruses, retroviruses, lentiviruses, flaviviruses, hepaciviruses, paramyxoviruses, and her- pesviruses, with the notable exclusion of gamma- and delta-retro- viruses. Interestingly, GRFT is also effective against the non- enveloped human papillomavirus (HPV), where it acts during a late step in the viral entry process rather than during initial attachment (O’Keefe et al., 2010; Lusvarghi and Bewley, 2016). In vivo administration of GRFT demonstrated clear therapeutic effi- cacy, significantly mitigating disease severity and reducing mortality in lethal SARS-CoV infection models (O’Keefe et al., 2010). Highlighting its strong translational potential, GRFT has also advanced to phase I clinical trials against human immunodeficiency virus (HIV-1) infections (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifiers: NCT04032717, NCT02875119). In addition to potent inhibition of ANDV entry (Shrivastava-Ranjan et al., 2020), found that a synthetic trimeric variant (3mGRFT) possessing nine oligosaccha- ride-binding sites demonstrated even greater in vitro potency against ANDV and SNV. However, in contrast to its post-infection efficacy seen in other viral models (Lusvarghi and Bewley, 2016), the authors observed that GRFT lacked potent inhibitory activity against ANDV post-infection. While GRFT showed in vitro effec- tivity against New World hantaviruses (Shrivastava-Ranjan et al., 2020), the lectin inhibited HTNV in vivo and provided partial protection in suckling mice infected with HTNV (Zhao et al., 2022). Moreover, GRFT can be produced on a large scale and can be easily purified, highlighting its potential as an antiviral candidate for further preclinical testing against orthohantaviruses (Zhao et al., 2022). Exploring natural host defense proteins, bovine lactoferrin (LF) has demonstrated significant efficacy as a viral inhibitor against SEOV. LF prevents initial viral adsorption and adhesion, likely by interacting with cellular glycosaminoglycans such as heparin, or by sterically hindering the virus from binding to host b-integrin and lectin receptors (Murphy et al., 2000, 2001). Importantly, LF has no antiviral effect once the virus entered the host cell. In vivo, prophylactic administration of LF one day prior to orthohantavirus inoculation improved survival rates in mice up to 70% (at 160 mg/ kg), with a double-administration regimen enhancing survival to over 94%. Furthermore, when prophylactic LF treatment was combined with subsequent ribavirin administration, the two agents functioned synergistically, profoundly reducing viral shed- ding and completely inhibiting viral protein expression (Murphy et al., 2000, 2001). Discovered through a high-throughput screening of over 2,300 approved drugs and traditional Chinese medicines, cepharanthine (CEP), which is a compound isolated from Stephania cephalantha Hayata, has emerged as a highly potent viral entry and membrane fusion inhibitor. In vitro, CEP inhibited HTNV pseudovirus (EC50 value of 0.9 μM) and reduced viral nucleic acid copies by 73% at 20 μM. In vivo, administering CEP to Balb/c mice five hours post- infection significantly reduced infection by 93% (at 90 mg/kg/day) and 94% (at 180 mg/kg/day). Given its established safety profile, Kocabiyik et al. 10.3389/fcimb.2026.1972830 Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology frontiersin.org 03 CEP represents a high-priority candidate for repurposing and advancement into human clinical trials against orthohantaviruses (Wen et al., 2022). Viral replication and polymerase inhibitors Ribavirin (1-b- D-ribofuranosyl-1H-1,2,4-triazole-3- carboxamide; RBV), a synthetic guanosine nucleoside analogue, serves as the historical benchmark for anti-hantaviral therapy (Sidwell et al., 1972). Once it is transported into host cells, RBV is rapidly phosphorylated into metabolites such as RBV-5’-mono- phosphate (RBV-MP) and RBV-5’-triphosphate (RBV-TP). While RBV-MP inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH), resulting in a decrease in intracellular GTP levels, RBV-TP selectively interacts with the viral RdRp as its primary mechanism of action (Severson et al., 2003; Sun et al., 2007). The incorporation of RBV leads to accumulation of genomic errors, and thus to dramatic loss of virus viability (“error catastrophe”) (Severson et al., 2003; Chung et al., 2007). Preclinical evaluation confirmed that early RBV administration reduces viral loads and prevents severe disease in suckling mouse models infected with Hantaan virus (HTNV) and hamster models infected with Andes virus (ANDV) (Huggins et al., 1986; Ogg et al., 2013). Clinically, intravenous RBV demonstrated efficacy in a double-blind, placebo- controlled trial of 242 patients with HTNV-induced HFRS, signif- icantly reducing hemorrhagic and overall mortality (Huggins et al., 1991). However, efficacy varies significantly across strains and clinical syndromes. In the context of HCPS caused by Andes virus (ANDV), intervention with RBV eliminated mortality com- pared to a 35% historical case-fatality rate and reduced the inci- dence of the severe cardiopulmonary phase from 84% to 57% (Strella et al., 2025). Conversely, in a larger placebo-controlled, double-blinded trial evaluating intravenous RBV for HCPS, the drug failed to demonstrate overall therapeutic efficacy, revealing no significant difference in survival (70% with RBV vs. 62% with placebo), nor in necessity of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) between groups (Mertz et al., 2004). Trials in HFRS caused by Puumala virus (PUUV) also showed insufficient efficacy and safety of intravenous RBV, likely due to delayed drug administra- tion and weaker correlation between viral load and disease severity compared to HTNV infection (Malinin and Platonov, 2017). Despite its status as an established treatment for HFRS, the clinical utility of RBV is constrained by dose-limiting toxicities, most notably reversible hemolytic anemia, reported in 71% of recipients (Chapman et al., 1999; Jonsson et al., 2010). Furthermore, the lack of efficacy in HCPS and PUUV-caused HFRS is attributed to the rapid clinical progression of these diseases, which often leaves a narrow window for intervention before the onset of irreversible organ failure (Heyman et al., 2009; Vaheri et al., 2013a; Strella et al., 2025). Originally discovered by Toyama Chemical Co., Ltd., during a screening for anti-influenza compounds, the prodrug favipiravir (T- 705) has emerged as a potent viral replication inhibitor. Upon cellular entry, host enzymes convert favipiravir into its active form, favipiravir-RTP. This active metabolite functions as a purine nucleotide analogue that is incorporated into nascent viral RNA, inducing lethal mutagenesis in the viral genome (Furuta et al., 2009, 2017). Safronetz et al. (2013) have shown that favipiravir potently inhibited ANDV and SNV in vitro, and provided 100% survival in lethal ANDV hamster models when treatment was initiated before viremia, making it an important drug candidate for post-exposure prophylaxis. To further enhance clinical outcomes, Mayor et al. (2021) combined the use of favipiravir with ribavirin to achieve synergistic orthohantavirus inhibition. full_text_sections.full_text: Hantaviral therapeutics: life cycle targets and chemotherapeutic interventions Deren Zehra Kocabiyik 1,2, Jansen de Araujo 3, Edison Luiz Durigon 2,3* and Carsten Wrenger 1,2* 1Unit for Drug Discovery, Department of Parasitology, Institute of Biomedical Sciences, University of São Paulo, São Paulo, Brazil, 2Institut Pasteur de São Paulo, São Paulo, Brazil, 3Department of Microbiology, Institute of Biomedical Sciences, University of São Paulo, São Paulo, Brazil Orthohantaviruses represent a persistent global health threat, being responsible for life-threatening diseases such as Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) and Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS). Despite high case fatality rates and recent outbreaks, there are currently no universally licensed antivirals or vaccines. Clinical management remains heavily reliant on supportive care and repurposed drugs, which often exhibit limited efficacy and dose-limiting toxicities. This review examines rational drug design strategies targeting critical steps in the viral life cycle, specifically Gn/Gc-mediated cellular entry and RNA- dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp)-driven genome replication. We evaluate the current landscape of viral inhibitors, including peptidomimetics, nucleoside analogues, and naturally derived compounds. To accelerate the discovery of novel treatments, we advocate for the integration of modern in silico screening to evaluate extensive chemical and natural product libraries. These broad com- pound collections offer a structurally diverse and largely untapped reservoir for antiviral development. Ultimately, expanding preclinical testing to include globally neglected variants will be essential to develop broad-spectrum hantaviral ther- apeutics capable of mitigating future epidemic threats. KEYWORDS antiviral discovery, drug development, orthohantavirus, chemotherapeutics, phytochemicals, viral entry inhibitors, RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) inhibitors, viral life cycle targets Introduction The April 2026 Andes hantavirus outbreak on a cruise ship served as a reminder of the ongoing challenges pathogens pose to global public health (Andes Virus Outbreak Working Group, 2026; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2026; World Health Organization, 2026b). The high case fatality rate highlights that there are currently no universally licensed antivirals or vaccines against orthohantavirus infections (World Health Organization, 2026a). These rodent-borne pathogens belong to the family Hantaviridae, genus Orthohantavirus, and are enveloped, tri-segmented, single-stranded negative-sense RNA viruses (Jonsson et al., 2010). They cause two distinct, life-threatening clinical syndromes, one being Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) in Eurasia, and Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS) in the Americas (Heyman et al., 2009). papers.title: Hantavirus emergence through a One Health lens: ecological dynamics, human exposure and integrated surveillance
papers.abstract: Abstract Hantaviruses are rodent-borne zoonotic viruses that cause haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Eurasia and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in the Americas. Although human hantavirus infections are usually recognised clinically, infection risk is affected by upstream factors including reservoir-host ecology, environmental variability and human exposure. Evidence from China, Europe and the Americas shows that the incidence of hantavirus may depend on rodent population dynamics, climate conditions, land use, agricultural practices, housing environments and recreational or travel-related exposure. In China, the seasonal pattern of haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, including a major autumn–winter peak and a smaller spring or spring–summer peak in many endemic areas, illustrates how virus–host ecology and agricultural labour jointly affect the human risk. In Europe, bank vole population cycles have been shown to influence Puumala virus epidemics, while studies in the Americas have linked rainfall, rodent abundance and human exposure in domestic, occupational and recreational settings. This mini review synthesises evidence on the ecological drivers, exposure pathways and surveillance challenges for hantavirus diseases through a One Health lens. We suggest that One Health approaches should move beyond general calls for multisector collaboration towards evidence-informed surveillance linking rodent, environmental and human data to setting-specific prevention, such as issuing seasonal risk warnings and reinforcing exposure-reduction measures before harvest periods in endemic agricultural regions.

Hantavirus emergence through a One Health lens: ecological dynamics, human exposure and integrated surveillance Xinyu Wang1,2* Abstract Hantaviruses are rodent-borne zoonotic viruses that cause haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Eurasia and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in the Americas. Although human hantavirus infections are usually recognised clinically, infection risk is affected by upstream factors including reservoir-host ecology, environmental variability and human exposure. Evidence from China, Europe and the Americas shows that the incidence of hantavi- rus may depend on rodent population dynamics, climate conditions, land use, agricultural practices, housing environ- ments and recreational or travel-related exposure. In China, the seasonal pattern of haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, including a major autumn–winter peak and a smaller spring or spring–summer peak in many endemic areas, illustrates how virus–host ecology and agricultural labour jointly affect the human risk. In Europe, bank vole population cycles have been shown to influence Puumala virus epidemics, while studies in the Americas have linked rainfall, rodent abundance and human exposure in domestic, occupational and recreational settings. This mini review synthesises evidence on the ecological drivers, exposure pathways and surveillance challenges for hantavirus diseases through a One Health lens. We suggest that One Health approaches should move beyond general calls for multisec- tor collaboration towards evidence-informed surveillance linking rodent, environmental and human data to setting- specific prevention, such as issuing seasonal risk warnings and reinforcing exposure-reduction measures before har- vest periods in endemic agricultural regions. Keywords Hantavirus, One Health, Haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, Rodent reservoir, Ecological surveillance, China, Travel medicine Introduction The epidemiology of hantaviruses is tightly linked to res- ervoir hosts, environmental conditions and human expo- sure, making them a useful model for reviewing zoonotic emergence through a One Health lens. Medically impor- tant hantaviruses are maintained primarily in rodent reservoirs and are associated with two major human disease syndromes: haemorrhagic fever with renal syn- drome (HFRS), reported mainly in Europe and Asia, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS; also his- torically referred to as hantavirus pulmonary syndrome), reported mainly in the Americas [1–3]. Human infec- tion is usually accidental and occurs when people enter environments contaminated by infectious rodent excreta; however, Andes virus remains the major exception, with documented person-to-person transmission under con- ditions of close or prolonged contact [3, 4]. Rather than cataloguing hantavirus species, this review focuses on synthesising the evidence for how ecological *Correspondence: Xinyu Wang snowmed@gmail.com 1 Department of Infectious Diseases, Huashan Hospital, Fudan University, Shanghai 200040, China 2 National Medical Center for Infectious Diseases, Shanghai 200040, China Page 2 of 7 Wang ﻿One Health Advances (2026) 4:36 and social processes shape human infection. Key ques- tions are not only which virus is carried by which rodent, but under what environmental and behavioural condi- tions infected reservoirs and susceptible humans are brought into contact. This framing is relevant for the One Health approach, because hantavirus risk can be exam- ined across measurable links including the rodent popu- lation density, reservoir-infection prevalence, climate variability, land use, agricultural or occupational expo- sure, housing conditions, recreational travel and clinical surveillance [1, 5]. China’s long-standing HFRS experi- ence, Europe’s cyclic Puumala virus epidemics and HCPS outbreaks in the Americas collectively provide comple- mentary evidence for understanding hantavirus emer- gence as an integrated human–animal–environment problem. This makes hantavirus disease a useful case for examining how the One Health approach can move from a conceptual framework to measurable surveillance indi- cators and setting-specific prevention. Reservoir ecology and environmental drivers of hantavirus risk The geographic distribution of hantavirus infection is strongly affected by its reservoir-host ecology. Although an increasing variety of hantaviruses have been detected in mammals, medically important hantaviruses are mainly maintained in rodent reservoirs, and many patho- genic viruses show close associations with particular host species or host complexes [1, 2]. This host dependence helps to explain the geographically uneven hantavirus risk, with human disease only occurring where compe- tent reservoirs, suitable habitats and human exposure all overlap. However, reservoir presence alone is insuf- ficient to predict human risk, and the local incidence also depends on rodent abundance, infection prevalence within reservoir populations, seasonal movement, habi- tat disturbance and the frequency with which humans enter contaminated environments [5]. Environmental variability can influence hantavirus transmission by changing the reservoir-host population dynamics and human–rodent contact. Increased rain- fall may enhance vegetation growth and food availabil- ity for rodents, thus supporting their reproduction and survival, while drought, habitat disruption or cold stress may drive rodents into human dwellings, storage areas or workplaces. The Four Corners region of the southwestern United States remains a classic example, where El Niño- associated precipitation led to ecological conditions that favoured increases in deer mouse populations, with a subsequent marked increase in HCPS cases in affected areas [6]. In Europe, Puumala virus epidemics have been linked to bank vole population cycles influenced by for- est ecology, food availability and seasonal conditions [7]. These examples suggest that climate is not a direct cause in isolation, but can influence risk via reservoir ecology and exposure pathways. Because human hantavirus cases often occur after changes in reservoir populations, rodent abundance and infection prevalence can act as early-warning indicators. Long-term ecological studies in Europe and the Americas have shown that rodent population cycles may precede changes in human disease risk [6, 7]. In China, ecologi- cal studies of HFRS have also emphasised the interacting roles of environmental variability, reservoir ecology and human behaviour in shaping disease dynamics [5]. These findings support a practical One Health implication: rodent monitoring should not be treated solely as ecolog- ical research, but as part of an integrated risk-assessment system linking animal, environmental and human health data. Land use, agriculture and human exposure: evidence from China and beyond Land use determines how often reservoir hosts, con- taminated environments and susceptible humans share the same space. Agricultural expansion, crop harvesting, grain storage, peri-domestic farming structures, forest edges and poorly sealed rural housing can increase the opportunities for contact with rodent excreta. A system- atic review of land cover, land use and human hantavi- rus infection risk found that agricultural land use was positively associated with infection risk in several set- tings, particularly in China and Brazil, whereas associa- tions with forest cover, grassland or built-up areas varied by region and virus ecology [8]. This heterogeneity is important, in that land use is not a universal risk factor but rather modifies exposure through local combinations of reservoir species, farming systems, housing conditions and human behaviour. China provides one of the clearest examples of how virus ecology and human activity jointly structure hanta- virus seasonality. In many endemic areas, HFRS shows a bimodal pattern, with a larger autumn–winter peak and a smaller spring or spring–summer peak. In China, this bimodal pattern has often been interpreted as reflect- ing the coexistence of different virus–host systems and exposure settings. Hantaan virus, mainly associated with Apodemus agrarius, contributes more to field or rural exposure and autumn–winter incidence, whereas Seoul virus, carried by Rattus norvegicus, is more relevant to peri-domestic or urban transmission and spring inci- dence in many settings [9–11]. In Zibo City, HFRS cases peaked during March–May and October–December, illustrating the seasonal human risk pattern [9]. Spatial analyses from the same region further suggested that Page 3 of 7 Wang ﻿One Health Advances (2026) 4:36 spring and autumn risks differed geographically, support- ing targeted seasonal prevention [12]. The link between agricultural activity and HFRS sea- sonality is particularly evident in high-incidence prov- inces such as Shandong. A time-series analysis reported marked seasonality and discussed the temporal cor- respondence between agricultural activity and HFRS incidence: the autumn harvest usually begins in late September, cases then rise rapidly in October, peak in November, and decline in December [13]. The incubation period of hantavirus infection suggests that this pattern is biologically plausible and consistent with exposure dur- ing harvesting, field work, grain handling or temporary accommodation in rodent-infested settings. Together with the smaller spring peak observed in many endemic areas, this pattern suggests that HFRS risk is shaped by seasonally changing combinations of reservoir ecology, agricultural labour and peri-domestic exposure, rather than by a single constant pathway. In addition to agriculture, hantavirus exposure may occur in occupational, domestic, recreational and travel settings. Farmers, forestry workers, construction work- ers, cleaners, military personnel and people entering rodent-infested buildings may experience intense short- term exposure when contaminated dust is disturbed. Recreational exposure can occur when visitors stay in cabins, campsites or enclosed structures with rodent infestation. The 2012 Yosemite National Park outbreak, linked to overnight stays in insulated tent cabins, showed how built environments can convert local rodent ecology into visitor risk [14]. The 2026 cruise-associated Andes virus cluster illustrates a different pathway, with local ecological exposure potentially becoming a multi-coun- try public health problem when combined with delayed recognition, confined travel settings and international movements [15]. Surveillance evidence and gaps across human– animal–environment systems China’s long-term HFRS experience provides an instruc- tive example of surveillance that already contains several One Health elements, even if not always labelled as such. National surveillance has combined human case report- ing with rodent surveillance, laboratory testing and tar- geted prevention in endemic areas. During 2006–2012, 77,558 HFRS cases and 866 deaths were reported in China. Cases were clustered in a small number of prov- inces and occurring mainly in spring and autumn–win- ter seasons, with farmers remaining the largest affected occupational group [10]. More recent national data for 2014–2023 show continuing geographic and virological complexity, with Hantaan virus, Seoul virus and Puu- mala virus among the identified human HFRS-associated hantaviruses in China [11]. These regional contrasts are summarised in Table 1, which compares rodent, envi- ronmental and human surveillance components across China, Europe and the Americas. Despite the value of long-term case reporting, human surveillance alone is inherently too late for hantavirus prevention, and human cases usually only appear after ecological changes, rodent population shifts and expo- sure events have already occurred. Clinical recogni- tion may also be delayed because the early symptoms are non-specific and overlap with leptospirosis, dengue, influenza-like illness, malaria, COVID-19 and other febrile syndromes [3]. This is particularly relevant in rural or travel-related settings, where the exposure event may be remote in time and place from the diagnosis. For surveillance to support prevention rather than only documentation, clinical signals should be connected with rodent, environmental and exposure information. In clinical practice, a compatible syndrome combined with a carefully reconstructed exposure history—such as recent rural residence, crop harvesting, cleaning of rodent-infested spaces, cabin stay or expedition travel— may provide the first actionable signal before laboratory confirmation. The One Health challenge is therefore not simply to collect more data, but to link the appropriate data to timely decisions. Information on rodent density, reser- voir infection prevalence, climate anomalies, agricultural calendars, land-use changes, clinical syndromes and travel or occupational histories is often held by different sectors and interpreted separately. Broader One Health early-warning literature emphasises the importance of bottom-up reporting and grassroots actors for reduc- ing delays between outbreak emergence, notification and response [16]. For hantavirus diseases, integrated early warning should therefore be judged not by the number of assembled datasets, but by whether ecological and clinical signals lead to earlier, setting-specific preven- tion. Future surveillance should therefore be built around predefined risk questions and response thresholds rather than around parallel human, animal and environmental datasets. In resource-limited settings, integrated One Health surveillance should not aim to monitor every possible ecological, animal and human indicator. A more feasible approach is to develop a minimum surveillance package tailored to local risk settings, combining routine report- ing of compatible human syndromes, simple rodent-den- sity indicators, seasonal agricultural calendars, rainfall or flooding alerts, community reports of rodent infestation and exposure histories collected during clinical assess- ment. Standardised metrics could include monthly rodent density, the proportion of captured rodents test- ing positive, rainfall deviation from the seasonal baseline, the number of compatible human cases, the proportion with documented exposure history and the number of high-risk settings receiving seasonal risk communication. Institutional coordination could be organised through periodic joint risk assessment meetings involving public health, clinical, agricultural, veterinary, environmental and travel or tourism sectors, with each warning signal linked to predefined prevention measures. Figure 1 illus- trates this proposed framework by linking ecological early-warning indicators to clinical decision nodes and public health actions. However, reservoir presence alone is insuf- ficient to predict human risk, and the local incidence also depends on rodent abundance, infection prevalence within reservoir populations, seasonal movement, habi- tat disturbance and the frequency with which humans enter contaminated environments [5]. Environmental variability can influence hantavirus transmission by changing the reservoir-host population dynamics and human–rodent contact. Increased rain- fall may enhance vegetation growth and food availabil- ity for rodents, thus supporting their reproduction and survival, while drought, habitat disruption or cold stress may drive rodents into human dwellings, storage areas or workplaces. The Four Corners region of the southwestern United States remains a classic example, where El Niño- associated precipitation led to ecological conditions that favoured increases in deer mouse populations, with a subsequent marked increase in HCPS cases in affected areas [6]. In Europe, Puumala virus epidemics have been linked to bank vole population cycles influenced by for- est ecology, food availability and seasonal conditions [7]. These examples suggest that climate is not a direct cause in isolation, but can influence risk via reservoir ecology and exposure pathways. Because human hantavirus cases often occur after changes in reservoir populations, rodent abundance and infection prevalence can act as early-warning indicators. Long-term ecological studies in Europe and the Americas have shown that rodent population cycles may precede changes in human disease risk [6, 7]. In China, ecologi- cal studies of HFRS have also emphasised the interacting roles of environmental variability, reservoir ecology and human behaviour in shaping disease dynamics [5]. These findings support a practical One Health implication: rodent monitoring should not be treated solely as ecolog- ical research, but as part of an integrated risk-assessment system linking animal, environmental and human health data. papers.title: Human Orthohantavirus infections: From virology and clinical epidemiology to oral biological features and dental practice
papers.abstract: Abstract Hantaviruses are rodent-borne zoonotic pathogens responsible for 2 severe clinical syndromes in humans: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), affecting an estimated 150,000 to 200,000 individuals annually worldwide, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), characterized by fulminant pulmonary edema with case fatality rates approaching 40%. Although the systemic manifestations of hantavirus disease are well described, the oral and salivary dimensions of infection have received comparatively little attention in the dental literature. This review synthesizes current evidence on the virology, global epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, oral complications, diagnostic approaches, treatment options, and dental practice implications of human hantavirus infections. A narrative review with a structured search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar was conducted, supplemented by hand-searching and by consultation of the World Health Organization and European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control outbreak reporting. Particular attention was directed toward primary research on salivary immunity, oral fluid diagnostics, and salivary gland tropism. Andes virus (ANDV) antigen has been detected in secretory cells of human salivary glands, and ANDV uniquely resists the antiviral capacity of human saliva, providing a biologically plausible mechanism for its person-to-person transmissibility. Infectious virus has since been recovered from saliva and gingival crevicular fluid during acute infection, although a salivary route of transmission remains an epidemiological association rather than proven. In a cohort of 69 confirmed ANDV-infected cases, salivary secretory immunoglobulin A (sIgA) was significantly elevated (4.846 vs. 0.333 mg/mL in exposed-uninfected contacts), whereas mucins MUC7 and MUC5B were more frequently detected in exposed-but-not-infected household contacts, a cross-sectional finding whose direction of causation is unresolved. Total salivary sIgA is a non-specific marker of mucosal immune activation and has no pathogen specificity. Oral fluid IgM assays for Hantaan virus achieved 96.7% sensitivity and 94.9% specificity against serum reference, supporting further evaluation of non-invasive salivary surveillance. Clinically, severe sore throat persisting for 2 to 3 weeks and oropharyngeal edema are documented as early features of hantavirus infection. Thrombocytopenia, which may be profound during the oliguric phase of HFRS, confers significant oral hemorrhagic risk. Human hantavirus infection presents with clinically significant oral and salivary manifestations that are directly relevant to dental practitioners. Dental teams should be aware of the hemorrhagic risk in patients with thrombocytopenia, the aerosol risk in patients with HCPS, the theoretical risk of ANDV transmission via oral contact in endemic regions, and the emerging utility of salivary diagnostics. Recommendations for dental practice are extrapolated from medical, virological, and general infection control evidence, rather than from dental clinical research, and are identified as precautionary where that is the case.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, affecting up to 200,000 people annually worldwide; oral and salivary dimensions of infection have received little attention in dental literature.
analysis.methods: Narrative review with a structured search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and WHO/ECDC outbreak reports, focusing on primary research about salivary immunity, oral fluid diagnostics, and salivary gland tropism.
analysis.results: ANDV antigen was detected in secretory cells of human salivary glands and infectious virus recovered from saliva and gingival crevicular fluid; salivary sIgA was markedly elevated in infected cases (4.846 vs 0.333 mg/mL); oral‑fluid IgM assay for Hantaan virus showed 96.7 % sensitivity and 94.9 % specificity; severe sore throat, oropharyngeal edema, and thrombocytopenia‑related oral hemorrhage are early clinical features.
analysis.contribution: Highlights oral and salivary manifestations directly relevant to dental practice and supports salivary diagnostics as a non‑invasive surveillance tool.
analysis.limitations: Salivary transmission remains an epidemiological association rather than proven; recommendations are precautionary and not derived from dental clinical research; the review is based only on abstract‑level evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause HFRS and HCPS, affecting up to 200,000 people yearly; oral and salivary aspects are understudied. Methods: Narrative review with structured searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar and WHO/ECDC reports, emphasizing salivary immunity and diagnostics. Results: ANDV antigen found in salivary gland cells and infectious virus recovered from saliva; sIgA higher in infected cases (4.846 vs 0.333 mg/mL); oral‑fluid IgM assay for Hantaan virus achieved 96.7 % sensitivity and 94.9 % specificity; early oral signs include severe sore throat, edema, and thrombocytopenia‑related hemorrhagic risk. Contribution: Identifies oral manifestations relevant to dental care and supports salivary testing for surveillance. Limitations: Salivary transmission is an association, not proven; recommendations are precautionary and not based on dental clinical trials; only abstract data were reviewed.

papers.title: Multi-host circulation and evolutionary dynamics of hantaviruses in small mammals in Southwestern China
papers.abstract: China represents a major hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS)-endemic region, where small mammals, particularly rodents, constitute the principal reservoir hosts. This study characterized HV diversity, RNA detection rate, host range, evolutionary history, and tissue distribution in 1 717 wild small mammals collected from Yunnan Province, China. HVs were detected in 47 animals, corresponding to an overall RNA detection rate of 2.74% (47/1 717, 95% CI: 1.97%–3.51%). At least five HV species or lineages were identified across 10 small mammal species, including Orthohantavirus luxiense (LUXV), Orthohantavirus fugongense (FUGV), Orthohantavirus seoulense (SEOV), Orthohantavirus caobangense (CBNV), and Thottimvirus sp. Host‐virus coevolutionary analysis suggested extensive interspecies transmission, with particularly strong support for phylogenetically inferred host‐switching events involving SEOV and FUGV. Preliminary analysis of tissue viral loads revealed that LUXV was widely distributed across various tissues and that significant differences in viral levels existed among tissues (χ2 = 27.500, P < 0.001). Collectively, these findings elucidate the genetic diversity and evolutionary dynamics of HVs in small mammals in Yunnan.

analysis.summary_en: Background: China is a major HFRS‑endemic region where small mammals, especially rodents, are the main reservoir hosts. Methods: The study sampled 1 717 wild small mammals from Yunnan Province, China, and used RT‑PCR to assess hantavirus RNA presence. Results: HV RNA was detected in 47 animals (2.74% detection rate, 95% CI: 1.97–3.51%), with five HV species/lineages identified across 10 mammal species; host‑virus coevolution analysis indicated extensive interspecies transmission, especially between SEOV and FUGV, and LUXV showed widespread tissue distribution with significant inter‑tissue viral load differences (χ² = 27.500, P < 0.001). Contribution: The study reveals hantavirus genetic diversity and evolutionary dynamics in Yunnan’s small mammals, informing surveillance and public‑health strategies. Limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

papers.title_zh: 中国西南地区小型哺乳动物中汉坦病毒es的多宿主循环与进化动态

analysis_zh.background: 中国是肾综合征出血热的主要流行地区,小型哺乳动物,尤其是啮齿动物,是主要的储存宿主。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究在中国云南省采集了1 717只野生小型哺乳动物,并使用RT‐PCR检测汉坦病毒(汉坦病毒)RNA的存在。
analysis_zh.results: 在47只动物中检测到汉坦病毒RNA,总检测率为2.74%(95%置信区间:1.97–3.51%)。在10种哺乳动物中鉴定出5种汉坦病毒种或系,包括LUXV、FUGV、首尔病毒、CBNV以及一种Thottimvirus属病毒;宿主‐病毒共进化分析提示存在广泛的跨种传播,尤其是首尔病毒与FUGV之间。LUXV表现出广泛的组织分布,并且不同组织间的病毒载量差异显著(χ2 = 27.500,P < 0.001)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 研究结果揭示了云南小型哺乳动物中汉坦病毒es的遗传多样性和进化动态,突出跨种传播和组织嗜性,为监测和公共卫生策略提供依据。
analysis_zh.limitations: 在提供的证据中未报告。

papers.title: Vaccines Against Hantavirus Infections: A Systematic Literature Review
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Hantaviruses infections are responsible for a hemorrhagic fever with renal and cardiopulmonary syndrome with case-fatality rates up to 50%. While inactivated vaccines are already available in China and South Korea, several additional candidate vaccines are under development. This systematic review summarizes the current clinical evidence on immunogenicity and short-term safety of vaccines targeting different hantavirus strains. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a systematic literature search was carried out to identify randomized and nonrandomized trials of any phase. Data were synthesized narratively within strata defined by vaccine platform, target virus, assay, immunogenicity and safety. Results: Ten trials on 961 adults were included: four single-arm trials on the inactivated vaccine and six early-phase DNA-vaccine trials. One month after last dose, the inactivated vaccine achieved neutralizing seropositivity by PRNT50 in 45.1% of the tested subjects after two priming doses and 55.7% after three, while the corresponding binding-antibody values measured by IFA were 87.3% and 95.7%. Among DNA vaccines, homologous responses reached 100% against HTNV and 83.3% against PUUV with monovalent constructs, whereas dual responses to the bivalent construct were registered in 33.3% and 77.8% of the subjects, when measured through PRNT50 and PsVNA50, respectively. One serious adverse event occurred, most likely unrelated to vaccination. Conclusions: No serious safety signal was identified, although safety remains insufficiently characterized. Measured immunogenicity depends as much on the assay as on the vaccine, and, in the absence of a validated correlate of protection, it cannot be read as a clinical benefit. Future research should prioritize validated correlates of protection and innovative trial designs adapted to low-incidence diseases.

analysis.background: Hantavirus infections cause hemorrhagic fever with renal and cardiopulmonary syndrome and can have case-fatality rates up to 50% (A1).
analysis.main_directions: The review discusses licensed inactivated vaccines in China and South Korea and multiple DNA vaccine candidates, organized by platform, target virus, immunogenicity assay, and safety (A2).
analysis.current_state: Ten trials (961 adults) show inactivated vaccines achieve 45.1%–55.7% neutralizing seropositivity and 87.3%–95.7% binding‑antibody positivity; DNA vaccines reach up to 100% homologous responses for HTNV and variable responses for PUUV and bivalent constructs; safety is acceptable with one serious adverse event deemed likely unrelated (A6, A7, A8, A9, A10, A11).
analysis.gaps: Immunogenicity results depend on assay choice, no validated correlate of protection exists, and safety data remain insufficiently characterized (A10, A11).
analysis.future_research: Future work should prioritize establishing validated correlates of protection and employing innovative trial designs suited to low‑incidence hantavirus diseases (A12).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infections cause hemorrhagic fever with renal and cardiopulmonary syndrome and up to 50% fatality. Main directions: The review examines licensed inactivated vaccines in China/Korea and DNA vaccine candidates, organized by platform, target virus, immunogenicity assays, and safety. Current state: Ten trials (961 adults) show inactivated vaccines reach 45–56% neutralizing seropositivity and >85% binding antibodies; DNA vaccines achieve up to 100% homologous responses for HTNV and variable responses for PUUV and bivalent constructs; safety is acceptable with one serious adverse event likely unrelated. Gaps: Immunogenicity is assay‑dependent, no validated correlate of protection, and safety data are limited. Future research: Develop validated correlates of protection and adopt innovative trial designs for low‑incidence hantavirus disease.

papers.title: Transmission timing and containment risk in human Andes virus outbreaks
papers.abstract: Abstract The 2026 multinational Andes virus (ANDV) outbreak linked to cruise-ship travel from Argentina triggered extensive contact tracing and quarantine. Whether intervention on this scale was necessary or sufficient depends on the risk of onward transmission, which can be difficult to estimate early in an outbreak. Using transmission-pair data from the 2018–2019 outbreak in Epuyén, Argentina, and a mechanistic model linking viral growth, symptom onset, and transmission, we estimated that 42.4% (95% CrI: 18.2–69.7%) of transmission occurs before symptom onset and that the median incubation period is 18.5 days (95% CrI: 16.5–19.5). We simulated outbreaks under an Epuyén-calibrated estimate (R = 2.12, k = 0.316) and a pooled estimate from 15 prior ANDV investigations (R = 0.24, k = 0.39), with intervention beginning after two generations, as in the cruise-associated event. Under the higher-transmission scenario, missing 10% of exposed individuals or downstream contacts resulted in a 29.9% probability of continued spread and a 20.6% probability that at least 5,000 ultimately uninfected people would be quarantined. Under lower transmission, continued spread stayed below 8%. However, the risk of onward transmission could not be estimated precisely from the first several detected cases. These findings therefore support rapid, comprehensive contact tracing and quarantine after large international exposure events despite substantial costs.

Using transmission-pair data from the 2018–2019 outbreak in Epuyén, Argentina, and a mechanistic model linking viral growth, symptom onset, and transmission, we estimated that 42.4% (95% CrI: 18.2–69.7%) of transmission occurs before symptom onset and that the median incubation period is 18.5 days (95% CrI: 16.5–19.5). We simulated outbreaks under an Epuyén-calibrated estimate (R = 2.12, k = 0.316) and a pooled estimate from 15 prior ANDV investigations (R = 0.24, k = 0.39), with intervention beginning after two generations, as in the cruise-associated event. Under the higher-transmission scenario, missing 10% of exposed individuals or downstream contacts resulted in a 29.9% probability of continued spread and a 20.6% probability that at least 5,000 ultimately uninfected people would be quarantined. Under lower transmission, continued spread stayed below 8%. However, the risk of onward transmission could not be estimated precisely from the first several detected cases. These findings therefore support rapid, comprehensive contact tracing and quarantine after large international exposure events despite substantial costs.

Introduction Andes virus (ANDV) is the only hantavirus known to be capable of person-to-person transmission, although documented transmission has been confined to a small number of localized outbreaks [1– 3]. ANDV infection is associated with a case-fatality rate of approximately 36% [4], and there are currently no approved vaccines or specific antiviral therapies. Recent increases in ANDV activity in South America have heightened concern about the potential for person-to-person spread [5]. In 2026, a multinational ANDV exposure event linked to cruise-ship travel from Argentina led to 13 reported cases and 3 deaths, and prompted extensive international contact tracing and prolonged quarantine of 147 passengers and crew from 23 countries [6, 7]. The severity of ANDV disease and its potential for person-to-person spread may warrant such intensive responses, but evidence on their effectiveness and associated quarantine burden remains limited. Evaluating containment strategies requires a detailed understanding of ANDV transmission dy- namics. Decisions about the scale and duration of contact tracing and quarantine depend on incu- bation periods, the timing of infectiousness relative to symptom onset, and individual-level variation in transmission. Long incubation periods prolong monitoring and quarantine, transmission before symptom onset allows infected individuals to spread infection before they are recognized and iso- lated, and variation in transmission means that a small number of infected individuals may account for a disproportionate share of secondary infections. However, estimating these quantities from outbreak data is complicated by evolving control measures, including case detection, isolation, and quarantine, which alter transmission opportunities over time. The 2018–2019 Epuyén outbreak provides the most detailed empirical data on person-to-person ANDV transmission. The original outbreak investigation reconstructed transmission chains, identi- fied superspreading, and estimated that the effective reproduction number (Re) declined from 2.12 before implementation of isolation and quarantine to 0.96 afterward [13]. Most reported ANDV infections, by contrast, arise from zoonotic spillover and are not followed by sustained person-to- person transmission. Transmission in Epuyén concentrated at a birthday party and a wake, in a town of fewer than 2,000 people, suggesting that what distinguishes these outcomes is not where infection is acquired but the number and intensity of close contacts during the brief window around symptom onset, variation in infectiousness across individuals, or both. The relative contributions of contact and infectiousness cannot be resolved from existing investigations, which report secondary cases but not contacts that did not result in transmission. Because incubation can last several weeks, the setting an infected person occupies during the transmission window may differ substan- tially from the setting in which exposure occurred. Transmission potential can therefore vary among cases, locations, and generations of the same outbreak. More recently, a latent-time analysis of the Epuyén transmission-pair data jointly estimated unobserved infection times, generation intervals, transmission timing relative to source symptom onset, time-varying reproduction numbers, and offspring dispersion from interval-censored data [12]. However, it modeled incubation and transmission timing as separate empirical delay distributions rather than as outcomes of a shared within-host process. This limited its ability to represent 2 . Here, we extend the latent-time framework by integrating a mechanistic model that jointly links infection, symptom onset, and transmission [15]. We incorporate the resulting estimates in stochastic branching-process simulations of a multinational exposure event based on the initial timing and magnitude of the 2026 cruise-associated outbreak. Given the variation in transmission observed across past ANDV events, we simulate outbreaks in both high- and low-transmission settings. The high-transmission setting uses parameters estimated from the Epuyén investigation, whereas the low-transmission setting uses pooled estimates from 15 prior ANDV investigations. We estimate the level of contact tracing and quarantine required for containment and quantify the consequences of incomplete or delayed intervention. Results We fitted the within-host-informed latent-time model to 34 cases and 33 reconstructed source- recipient pairs from the 2018–2019 Epuyén outbreak in Argentina (Table 1; Figure 1). Transmission was concentrated near source symptom onset, with an estimated 42.4% of transmission events oc- curring before symptoms appeared (95% CrI: 18.2–69.7%). The median transmission time was 0.07 days after source symptom onset (95% CrI: (-0.20) to 0.30 days), and the central 95% of transmission events occurred from 0.85 days before to 2.02 days after source symptom onset (Figure 1A). The median incubation period was 18.50 days (95% CrI: 16.50–19.50 days), with a central 95% distributional interval of 7.50–35.50 days (Figure 1C). An estimated 95% of infections developed symptoms by 31.50 days (95% CrI: 29.50–35.50), and 99% by 39.50 days (95% CrI: 35.50–44.50). The median generation interval was 22.50 days (95% CrI: 20.50–23.50 days) (Figure 1B), and the median serial interval was 21.79 days (95% CrI: 21.28–22.18 days) (Figure 1D). Thus, exposed individuals may require several weeks of follow-up even though onward transmission is concentrated within a narrow window around symptom onset. These estimates were broadly consistent with previous analyses of the Epuyén outbreak while providing model-based inference of latent infection times and transmission timing relative to symptom onset (Supplementary Results). Median estimates are reported with 95% credible intervals (CrIs), reflecting uncertainty in the estimated population median. The central 95% interval summarizes the expected range across individual infections or transmission events. Transmission timing is reported relative to source symptom onset, with negative values indicating transmission before symptom onset. Panels show the inferred distributions of the (A) transmission timing relative to source symptom onset, (B) generation interval, (C) incubation period, and (D) serial interval. Solid curves represent posterior median densities, and shaded regions indicate the corresponding 95% credible intervals. Dashed vertical lines mark zero days. In panel A, negative values indicate transmission before source symptom onset; in panel D, negative values indicate that the recipient developed symptoms before the source case. To characterize the transmission conditions documented across settings, we analyzed 15 pub- lished ANDV investigations. A hierarchical negative-binomial model estimated a pooled reproduc- tion number of 0.24 (95% CrI: 0.12–0.48) and a shared dispersion parameter of 0.39 (95% CrI: 0.19–0.89), reflecting low average but highly variable realized transmission across this broader set of investigations. Together with the Epuyén-calibrated estimates (R=2.12, k=0.316), these results anchored an empirically informed range of ANDV transmission potential. Hereafter, we refer to simulations using the Epuyén and pooled parameterizations as the higher- and lower-transmission scenarios, respectively. The primary analysis reproduced the timing of the 2026 cruise-associated response, with inter- vention beginning on simulation day 35, 26 days after symptom onset in the first detected case. 4 . Tracing failures had substantially greater consequences under higher transmission (Figure 2A). When tracing missed 5%, 10%, 25%, or 50% of exposed individuals or downstream contacts, post-response transmission outside quarantine occurred in 18.9%, 29.9%, 51.1%, and 70.8% of simulations, respectively. Under the lower transmission, this probability ranged from 0.7% with 5% missed to 7.8% with 50% missed. Among simulations with higher transmission and at least one additional post-response infection, missing 10% of contacts resulted in a median of 5 additional infections and a 95th percentile of 49. With 25% or 50% missed, the medians increased to 8 and 27, respectively, and the 95th percentiles to 111 and 351. With lower transmission, the median remained between one and two across tracing levels (Figure 2B). Quarantine burdens were substantially lower under lower transmission (Figure 2C). With 10% of contacts missed, the median number of retrospectively uninfected downstream contacts quaran- tined was 313 (IQR 185–440), compared with 1,821 (IQR 720–4,161) under the higher-transmission scenario. At lower transmission, the median burden fell by 49%, from 329 with complete tracing to 167 with 50% of contacts missed, because outbreaks were small and fewer contacts were traced. At higher transmission, fewer quarantines per case were offset by larger outbreaks and more tracing events, leaving the median comparatively stable but increasing the risk of very large quarantine burdens. Most response activity ended within the initial six-week quarantine period, but breakthrough transmission occasionally prolonged the response under the higher-transmission scenario. With 10% of contacts missed, the median additional response duration was zero months, the 95th percentile was 1.61 months, and 0.2% of simulations required at least four additional months of response activity. With 50% missed, the median increased to 1.02 months and the 95th percentile to 5.01 months. With lower transmission, additional response duration remained near zero (Figure 2D). The multinational response to the 2026 cruise-associated outbreak was initiated after seven confirmed or suspected cases were identified. To assess the consequences of delayed intervention, we initiated contact tracing and quarantine after different numbers of cases had been reported, assuming 95% tracing completeness (Figure 3). Under higher transmission, delaying intervention from the first to the twentieth reported case increased the probability of at least 100 infections from 2.7% to 38.2% and of at least 500 infections from 2.1% to 14.0%. Median outbreak size increased from 1 to 72 infections, median quarantine burden from 2 to 500 individuals, and the probability of quarantining at least 1,000 individuals from 2.7% to 36.0%. Under lower transmission, outbreaks rarely reached the later intervention points: only 13 of 10,000 simulations reached 10 reported cases, and none reached 20. Outcomes following greater delays therefore could not be estimated precisely. Under active containment, most simulated outbreaks ended before enough cases were detected to estimate the reproduction number precisely. Estimates from the first few detected cases were highly uncertain, with broad 95% credible intervals that commonly included R = 1 under both transmission scenarios (Supplementary Figure 5). papers.title_zh: 人类 安第斯病毒 疫情的传播时机与遏制风险

analysis_zh.background: 2026年多国安第斯病毒(安第斯病毒)疫情与来自阿根廷的邮轮旅行相关,促使开展大规模接触者追踪和隔离,凸显了评估安第斯病毒人际传播风险的必要性。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者使用了2018–2019年阿根廷Epuyén疫情的传播配对数据以及将病毒增殖、症状出现和传播关联的机制模型,随后进行随机分支过程模拟,校准至Epuyén(R = 2.12,k = 0.316)以及来自15项先前安第斯病毒研究的合并估计(R = 0.24,k = 0.39)。
analysis_zh.results: 他们估计,42.4%(95% CrI = 18.2–69.7%)的传播发生在症状出现前,中位潜伏期为18.5天(95% CrI = 16.5–19.5)。在高传播情景下,漏检10%的暴露接触者会导致持续传播的概率为29.9%,并有20.6%的概率需要对≥5,000名未感染者进行隔离;在低传播情景下,持续传播的概率保持在8%以下。
analysis_zh.contribution: 这些结果支持在大型国际暴露事件后迅速、全面开展接触者追踪和隔离,尽管成本高昂。
analysis_zh.limitations: 从最初的几例检测病例中无法精确估计后续传播风险,且研究结果基于尚未同行评审的预印本。

papers.title: Hantavirus species detection from viral genome sequences using explainable artificial intelligence techniques
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are important zoonotic pathogens associated with severe human diseases, including hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. The World Health Organization (WHO) has recognized the importance of strengthening hantavirus surveillance and early detection because of their public health impact. Nevertheless, Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based approaches for hantavirus species identification from viral genome sequences remain largely unexplored. This study developed and evaluated an explainable AI-based approach for hantavirus species identification using viral genome sequence fragments representing six hantavirus species. A transformer-based genomic representation approach (DNABERT-2) was used to generate representations for various Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) models. Sequence redundancy was quantified before model development, and performance was assessed using a 99%-sequence-identity group-aware partitioning strategy with five-fold group-aware cross-validation and an independent internal test set. Direct sequence-similarity auditing confirmed that no sequence pair with ≥ 99% global nucleotide identity crossed the development and test boundary. LightGBM achieved the highest mean group-aware cross-validation performance, with an Accuracy and weighted F1-Score of 99.51%, Cohen’s Kappa coefficient of 99.41%, and Brier Score of 0.19%. On the independent internal test set, LightGBM achieved an Accuracy and weighted F1-Score of 99.25%. SHAP analysis identified influential nucleotide sequence tokens contributing to LightGBM predictions, while a separate DNABERT-2 attention-based analysis identified highly attended nucleotide sequence patterns within the genomic encoder. These findings demonstrate the potential of the proposed approach as an auxiliary method for post-sequencing hantavirus species identification, genomic surveillance, and sequence-based research.

The World Health Organization (WHO) has recognized the importance of strengthening hantavirus surveillance and early detection because of their public health impact. Nevertheless, Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based approaches for hantavirus species identifi­ cation from viral genome sequences remain largely unexplored. This study developed and evaluated an explain­ able AI-based approach for hantavirus species identification using viral genome sequence fragments represent­ ing six hantavirus species. A transformer-based genomic representation approach (DNABERT-2) was used to generate representations for various Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) models. Sequence redundancy was quantified before model development, and performance was assessed using a 99%-sequence- identity group-aware partitioning strategy with five-fold group-aware cross-validation and an independent inter­ nal test set. Direct sequence-similarity auditing confirmed that no sequence pair with ≥ 99% global nucleotide identity crossed the development and test boundary. LightGBM achieved the highest mean group-aware cross- validation performance, with an Accuracy and weighted F1-Score of 99.51%, Cohen’s Kappa coefficient of 99.41%, and Brier Score of 0.19%. On the independent internal test set, LightGBM achieved an Accuracy and weighted F1-Score of 99.25%. Article in Press Scientific Reports https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-75095-x Keywords Hantavirus · Species · Detection · Viral genome sequences · Explainable AI Introduction Hantaviruses are negative-sense, tri-segmented Ribonucleic Acid (RNA) viruses belonging to the family Hanta­ viridae1. They are zoonotic pathogens transmitted primarily to humans through inhalation of aerosolized excreta from infected rodent hosts1–3. More than 25 hantavirus species have been associated with human disease4, prin­ cipally causing two major clinical syndromes: Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS), predominantly associated with Old World hantaviruses, including Hantaan Orthohantavirus, Orthohantavirus Seoulense, Ortho­ hantavirus Puumalaense, and Orthohantavirus Dobravaense in Europe and Asia; and Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS), primarily associated with New World hantaviruses, including Sin Nombre Orthohantavirus and Orthohantavirus Andesense in the Americas4–6. Following an incubation period of approximately 2–4 weeks, both syndromes may initially present with a nonspecific febrile prodromal phase characterized by fever, myalgia, headache, and gastrointestinal symptoms, which can hinder early clinical recognition4,7. Treatment of hantavirus infection is primarily supportive because no widely approved specific antiviral ther­ apy is currently available. Timely recognition of infection may increase clinical awareness of potential complica­ tions and facilitate appropriate monitoring and supportive interventions. Post-mortem case reports have described patients who initially presented to emergency or primary care services with a nonspecific diagnosis of “viral syn­ drome”, without hantavirus infection being considered8–10. Progression to the cardiopulmonary phase of HCPS or the oliguric phase of HFRS is associated with an increased risk of severe complications, mortality, or persistent organ impairment8. Case fatality rates for HCPS can reach 30–50%, while HFRS accounts for tens of thousands of hospitalizations annually across Eurasia4. Disease severity may also differ among hantavirus species, further emphasizing the importance of accurate viral characterization4. Hantaviruses therefore remain important zoonotic pathogens of public health concern because of their potential for emergence, geographic expansion, and association with severe human disease11,12. The World Health Orga­ nization (WHO) has emphasized the importance of strengthening hantavirus surveillance, laboratory capacity, early detection, and outbreak response to reduce the public health impact of these infections13. Recent hantavirus events have further highlighted the need for timely epidemiological investigation, laboratory confirmation, and genomic characterization to support public health decision-making14. Accordingly, accurate characterization of circulating hantavirus species can contribute to genomic surveillance, investigation of viral diversity, and public health preparedness. Laboratory confirmation of hantavirus infection commonly relies on molecular and serological methods, including Reverse Transcription Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR) and serological assays, such as Immu­ noglobulin M Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (IgM ELISA)15,16. Following molecular detection, spe­ cies-level characterization can provide additional information for investigating epidemiological patterns, viral diversity, disease-associated differences, and transmission dynamics relevant to public health surveillance17,18. Hantavirus species identification may be performed using species-specific molecular assays or genomic sequence analysis19,20. The increasing availability of viral sequence data therefore provides opportunities for computational approaches that can support post-sequencing species identification. Artificial Intelligence (AI), including Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL), has increasingly been applied in medicine and healthcare data for tasks such as disease detection, diagnosis, and severity predic­ tion21–23. ML methods, such as Support Vector Machines (SVM), Random Forest (RF), Decision Tree (DT), and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), can model complex relationships within structured data and have been widely applied across clinical prediction tasks24–26. DL architectures, including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), have further expanded the ability to analyze high-dimensional Article in Press Scientific Reports https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-75095-x and sequential data21,27,28. More recently, transformer-based models pretrained on genomic sequences have pro­ vided an additional approach for generating contextual representations directly from nucleotide sequence data. Previous applications of AI to hantavirus research have predominantly focused on population-level outbreak or infection-risk prediction rather than species identification from viral nucleotide sequences29–31. For instance, Kazasidis et al. developed an SVM-based early-warning system for predicting annual Orthohantavirus Puuma­ laense outbreaks in Germany, achieving an accuracy of 82.8% using weather variables and beech flowering intensity29. Other computational studies have similarly examined associations among rodent population dynam­ ics, climatic variables, and human hantavirus case counts30,31. Clinical applications have also been investigated. Bulut and Klein developed Kantesti, a multilingual AI-assisted clinical decision-support system that analyzes routine blood-test results to estimate the risk of hantavirus infection32. Following deployment across 50,000 interpreted laboratory reports, the system identified three laboratory-confirmed hantavirus cases that had initially been misclassified by clinicians32. Nevertheless, these approaches address outbreak forecasting, infection-risk assessment, or detection rather than species identification from viral nucleotide sequences29–33. In contrast, AI-based analysis of viral nucleotide sequences has increasingly been investigated for other viruses. Rancati et al. developed DeepAutoCoV, an unsupervised deep autoencoder approach based on SARS- CoV-2 Spike sequences to identify emerging lineages and forecast those likely to become dominant, illustrating the potential of learned sequence representations for genomic surveillance34. Peng et al. developed ViraLM using a pretrained genome foundation model to identify viral sequences directly from nucleotide data, demonstrating the potential of foundation-model representations for viral sequence analysis35. More recently, Rancati et al. introduced SARITA, a generative language model trained on SARS-CoV-2 Spike S1 sequences that generated realistic sequences and reproduced evolutionary patterns associated with subsequently emerging variants36. Anal­ yses across European countries have also demonstrated associations between genomic sequencing activity and epidemiological indicators, further emphasizing the importance of sequence data within pathogen-surveillance frameworks37. Collectively, these studies illustrate the increasing use of AI and language-model-based sequence representations for viral identification, evolutionary analysis, lineage forecasting, and genomic surveillance; nev­ ertheless, corresponding applications to hantavirus species identification remain limited. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, no previous study has investigated AI-based hantavirus species identifi­ cation directly from viral nucleotide sequences while incorporating explainable AI (XAI) techniques for this task. Therefore, this study aimed to develop and evaluate multiple ML and DL models for post-sequencing hantavirus species identification using nucleotide sequence data and representations generated by a pretrained genomic transformer. XAI techniques were additionally incorporated to investigate sequence-level features contribut­ ing to model predictions and to provide complementary exploratory information regarding nucleotide sequence patterns emphasized by the genomic encoder. The proposed approach is intended for post-sequencing genomic analysis, surveillance, and research rather than for the initial diagnosis of hantavirus infection. The findings may contribute to future development of AI-assisted approaches for hantavirus species identification and sequence- based genomic investigation. Materials and methods Figure 1 presents the data-driven AI framework utilized in this study, encompassing dataset preparation, sequence preprocessing and representation generation, model development, performance evaluation, and explainability analysis. Dataset and data preprocessing The dataset comprised 2,571 hantavirus-positive patient-associated records with corresponding viral genome sequence fragments representing six hantavirus species38. The source dataset classified the positive records as Article in Press Scientific Reports https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-75095-x Bayou virus (Orthohantavirus Bayoui), Dobrava virus (Orthohantavirus dobravaense), Hantaan virus (Hantaan Orthohantavirus), Puumala virus (Orthohantavirus Puumalaense), Seoul virus (Orthohantavirus Seoulense), and Sin Nombre virus (Sin Nombre Orthohantavirus)1. The virus names provided in the source dataset were retained as species labels throughout this study. Each source record was associated with a dataset-specific identifier and one corresponding FASTA sequence record. The identifier consisted solely of a randomly assigned number used within the public dataset and did not correspond to an actual clinical or institutional patient identifier. No directly identifying patient information was available, and the accompanying patient-associated information was anonymous. The dataset included 426 Bayou, 427 Dobrava, 422 Hantaan, 431 Puumala, 435 Seoul, and 430 Sin Nombre records. The source documen­ tation did not provide a sequence-length distribution or specify whether the available viral sequences represented complete genomes, individual genomic segments, or partial sequence fragments. Hantavirus genomes comprise three RNA segments, designated small (S), medium (M), and large (L)1. Nev­ ertheless, the source dataset did not provide S-, M-, or L-segment annotations, genomic coordinates, original sequence-repository information, accession numbers, strain identifiers, or isolate identifiers.
