It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. The final edited version will replace it automatically. Hantavirus species detection from viral genome sequences using explainable artificial intelligence techniques Amir Sorayaie Azar · Anita Bagherzadeh Mohasefi · Fatemeh Mohammadi · Jamshid Bagherzadeh Mohasefi · Ali Ebrahimi · Fredrikke Christie Knudtzen · Uffe Kock Wiil Received: 30 July 2026 / Accepted: 5 October 2026 © The Author(s) 2026 Abstract Hantaviruses are important zoonotic pathogens associated with severe human diseases, including hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. The World Health Organization (WHO) has recognized the importance of strengthening hantavirus surveillance and early detection because of their public health impact. Nevertheless, Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based approaches for hantavirus species identifi­ cation from viral genome sequences remain largely unexplored. This study developed and evaluated an explain­ able AI-based approach for hantavirus species identification using viral genome sequence fragments represent­ ing six hantavirus species. A transformer-based genomic representation approach (DNABERT-2) was used to generate representations for various Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) models. Sequence redundancy was quantified before model development, and performance was assessed using a 99%-sequence- identity group-aware partitioning strategy with five-fold group-aware cross-validation and an independent inter­ nal test set. Direct sequence-similarity auditing confirmed that no sequence pair with ≥ 99% global nucleotide identity crossed the development and test boundary. LightGBM achieved the highest mean group-aware cross- validation performance, with an Accuracy and weighted F1-Score of 99.51%, Cohen’s Kappa coefficient of 99.41%, and Brier Score of 0.19%. On the independent internal test set, LightGBM achieved an Accuracy and weighted F1-Score of 99.25%. SHAP analysis identified influential nucleotide sequence tokens contributing to LightGBM predictions, while a separate DNABERT-2 attention-based analysis identified highly attended nucleotide sequence patterns within the genomic encoder. These findings demonstrate the potential of the pro­ posed approach as an auxiliary method for post-sequencing hantavirus species identification, genomic surveil­ lance, and sequence-based research. Article in Press Scientific Reports https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-75095-x Keywords Hantavirus · Species · Detection · Viral genome sequences · Explainable AI Introduction Hantaviruses are negative-sense, tri-segmented Ribonucleic Acid (RNA) viruses belonging to the family Hanta­ viridae1. They are zoonotic pathogens transmitted primarily to humans through inhalation of aerosolized excreta from infected rodent hosts1–3. More than 25 hantavirus species have been associated with human disease4, prin­ cipally causing two major clinical syndromes: Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS), predominantly associated with Old World hantaviruses, including Hantaan Orthohantavirus, Orthohantavirus Seoulense, Ortho­ hantavirus Puumalaense, and Orthohantavirus Dobravaense in Europe and Asia; and Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS), primarily associated with New World hantaviruses, including Sin Nombre Orthohantavirus and Orthohantavirus Andesense in the Americas4–6. Following an incubation period of approximately 2–4 weeks, both syndromes may initially present with a nonspecific febrile prodromal phase characterized by fever, myalgia, headache, and gastrointestinal symptoms, which can hinder early clinical recognition4,7. Treatment of hantavirus infection is primarily supportive because no widely approved specific antiviral ther­ apy is currently available. Timely recognition of infection may increase clinical awareness of potential complica­ tions and facilitate appropriate monitoring and supportive interventions. Post-mortem case reports have described patients who initially presented to emergency or primary care services with a nonspecific diagnosis of “viral syn­ drome”, without hantavirus infection being considered8–10. Progression to the cardiopulmonary phase of HCPS or the oliguric phase of HFRS is associated with an increased risk of severe complications, mortality, or persistent organ impairment8. Case fatality rates for HCPS can reach 30–50%, while HFRS accounts for tens of thousands of hospitalizations annually across Eurasia4. Disease severity may also differ among hantavirus species, further emphasizing the importance of accurate viral characterization4. Hantaviruses therefore remain important zoonotic pathogens of public health concern because of their potential for emergence, geographic expansion, and association with severe human disease11,12. The World Health Orga­ nization (WHO) has emphasized the importance of strengthening hantavirus surveillance, laboratory capacity, early detection, and outbreak response to reduce the public health impact of these infections13. Recent hantavirus events have further highlighted the need for timely epidemiological investigation, laboratory confirmation, and genomic characterization to support public health decision-making14. Accordingly, accurate characterization of circulating hantavirus species can contribute to genomic surveillance, investigation of viral diversity, and public health preparedness. Laboratory confirmation of hantavirus infection commonly relies on molecular and serological methods, including Reverse Transcription Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR) and serological assays, such as Immu­ noglobulin M Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (IgM ELISA)15,16. Following molecular detection, spe­ cies-level characterization can provide additional information for investigating epidemiological patterns, viral diversity, disease-associated differences, and transmission dynamics relevant to public health surveillance17,18. Hantavirus species identification may be performed using species-specific molecular assays or genomic sequence analysis19,20. The increasing availability of viral sequence data therefore provides opportunities for computational approaches that can support post-sequencing species identification. Artificial Intelligence (AI), including Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL), has increasingly been applied in medicine and healthcare data for tasks such as disease detection, diagnosis, and severity predic­ tion21–23. ML methods, such as Support Vector Machines (SVM), Random Forest (RF), Decision Tree (DT), and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), can model complex relationships within structured data and have been widely applied across clinical prediction tasks24–26. DL architectures, including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), have further expanded the ability to analyze high-dimensional Article in Press Scientific Reports https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-75095-x and sequential data21,27,28. More recently, transformer-based models pretrained on genomic sequences have pro­ vided an additional approach for generating contextual representations directly from nucleotide sequence data. Previous applications of AI to hantavirus research have predominantly focused on population-level outbreak or infection-risk prediction rather than species identification from viral nucleotide sequences29–31. For instance, Kazasidis et al. developed an SVM-based early-warning system for predicting annual Orthohantavirus Puuma­ laense outbreaks in Germany, achieving an accuracy of 82.8% using weather variables and beech flowering intensity29. Other computational studies have similarly examined associations among rodent population dynam­ ics, climatic variables, and human hantavirus case counts30,31.…

papers.title: Andes virus from the MV Hondius outbreak is highly pathogenic in hamsters and airborne shed
papers.abstract: In May 2026, an outbreak of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) caused by Andes virus (ANDV) was detected aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius, sparking public health measures in multiple countries. ANDV infections in humans are mostly sporadic, most often linked to exposure to infected rodents in South America, although small clusters of human cases, like the 2026 outbreak on the MV Hondius occur as well. It is not known whether virological factors may contribute to this distinct epidemiology, and no phenotypic characterisation of the newly emerged ANDV (ANDV2026) has been carried out to date. Here, using an ANDV isolate from a presymptomatic patient from the MV Hondius, we studied pathogenesis, identified sites of viral replication, characterized innate and adaptive immune responses, and quantified shedding in golden Syrian hamsters. ANDV2026 proved to be highly pathogenic in hamsters, causing severe pulmonary disease reminiscent of HPS. ANDV2026 triggered a delayed type-I IFN response and inflammatory response in the lungs consistent with the key pathological features of HPS, and we detected viral replication in both respiratory and extra-respiratory tissues, including the brain. Infected animals mounted neutralising antibodies and T cell responses, the latter directed predominantly against the L and N proteins. Importantly, ANDV2026-infected animals shed virus through multiple routes, and we detected infectious virus in air samplers connected to cages housing ANDV2026-infected hamsters. In contrast, control hamsters infected with a rodent-derived ANDV isolate (ANDV9717869) shed little virus and air samples were consistently negative. These findings consolidate established features of ANDV pathogenesis, while revealing properties not previously described. Phenotypic characterisation of patient-derived ANDV isolates in animal models can strengthen outbreak preparedness, identify markers of disease severity, and support the development of medical countermeasures.

It is not known whether virological factors may contribute to this distinct epidemiology, and no phenotypic characterisation of the newly emerged ANDV (ANDV2026) has been carried out to date. Here, using an ANDV isolate from a presymptomatic patient from the MV Hondius, we studied pathogenesis, identified sites of viral replication, characterized innate and adaptive immune responses, and quantified shedding in golden Syrian hamsters. ANDV2026 proved to be highly pathogenic in hamsters, causing severe pulmonary disease reminiscent of HPS. ANDV2026 triggered a delayed type-I IFN response and inflammatory response in the lungs consistent with the key pathological features of HPS, and we detected viral replication in both respiratory and extra-respiratory tissues, including the brain. Infected animals mounted neutralising antibodies and T cell responses, the latter directed predominantly against the L and N proteins. Importantly, ANDV2026-infected animals shed virus through multiple routes, and we detected infectious virus in air samplers connected to cages housing ANDV2026-infected hamsters. In contrast, control hamsters infected with a rodent-derived ANDV isolate (ANDV9717869) shed little virus and air samples were consistently negative. These findings consolidate established features of ANDV pathogenesis, while revealing properties not previously described. Phenotypic characterisation of patient-derived ANDV isolates in animal models can strengthen outbreak preparedness, identify markers of disease severity, and support the development of medical countermeasures.

papers.title: Design and in silico evaluation of PV-GNProtecta: an mRNA multi-epitope vaccine candidate against Puumala virus using immunoinformatics and structural analysis.
papers.abstract: Puumala virus (PUUV), the principal causative agent of nephropathia epidemica (NE), poses a significant public health threat due to its zoonotic transmission, renal complications, and the lack of an approved vaccine. In this study, an immunoinformatics-driven mRNA multi-epitope vaccine, PV-GNProtecta, was designed using conserved regions of the viral glycoprotein (G) and nucleoprotein (N). Highly antigenic, non-allergenic, and non-toxic T-cell and B-cell epitopes were identified and assembled with appropriate adjuvants to enhance immunogenicity. Population coverage analysis suggested broad HLA responsiveness across diverse populations. The vaccine construct exhibited favorable physicochemical properties, including stability, solubility, and antigenicity. Structural validation predicted high model quality, with 95.5% of residues located in favored Ramachandran regions and an ERRAT score of 91.4. Molecular docking and MM-GBSA analyses predicted favorable computational interactions between PV-GNProtecta and TLR4, while a 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation provided computational insights into the dynamic behavior of the vaccine-TLR4 complex. Codon optimization suggested compatibility of the designed sequence with an Escherichia coli-based expression framework. Immune simulation predicted potential humoral and cellular immune response patterns, including changes in IgG, IFN-γ, and IL-2 levels. The designed mRNA sequence exhibited favorable predicted secondary structural characteristics; however, further experimental evaluation is required to assess translational efficiency and stability. Although this study is limited to computational analyses and requires experimental validation, the findings suggest that PV-GNProtecta may represent a potential candidate for further investigation against PUUV infection.

Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s44342-026-00081-8. Introduction Nephropathia epidemica (NE) is attributed to Puumala virus (PUUV), a naturally occurring form of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in humans, which is a zoonotic infectious disease and generally considered a mild-to-moderate form of hantavirus infection within the HFRS spectrum. PUUV (Puumala orthohantavirus) is classified within the genus Orthohantavirus, family Hantaviridae, and order Bunyavirales, as defined by current ICTV taxonomy, and it was previously grouped under the family Bunyaviridae prior to taxonomic reclassification. PUUV infection presents with highly variable outcomes, ranging from subclinical cases (70–80%) to severe HFRS, and carries a fatality rate of about 0.1%. PUUV infection commonly presents with sudden fever, headache, back pain, nausea, gastrointestinal symptoms, thrombocytopenia, hematuria, and varying degrees of acute kidney impairment. In some patients, additional manifestations such as blurred vision, dizziness, insomnia, respiratory complications, oliguria, and subsequent polyuria during recovery may also occur. Although PUUV infection is generally considered mild, severe complications can occur in a subset of patients, including acute kidney failure, hypotension, shock, pulmonary edema, Guillain-Barré syndrome, respiratory distress, disseminated intravascular coagulopathy (DIC), myocarditis, encephalitis, pituitary hemorrhage, seizures, and, in rare cases, multiorgan failure or fatal cerebral hemorrhage. The first identification of PUUV occurred in the early 1980s when the virus was isolated from bank voles (Myodes glareolus) in the Puumala region of Finland. Between July 1989 and June 1996, Finland reported 6701 PUUV infection cases confirmed via serological assays, with the highest incidence in the Itä-Savo district and a mortality rate below 0.1%, and later from 1995 to 2008, 22,681 cases were recorded with an average annual incidence of 31 per 100,000 population, resulting in 13 deaths and 52% of patients requiring hospitalization. PUUV accounts for approximately 93% of all notified hantavirus infections in Germany and caused a major outbreak in 2007 in Baden-Württemberg with 1089 reported human cases, while the highest annual number of PUUV infections in Germany was recorded in 2010 since hantavirus surveillance began in 2001. Also in 2007, Sweden’s Västerbotten County experienced a surprisingly severe outbreak of PUUV infection, with NE rates hitting 313 cases per 100,000 residents. Between 2001 and 2017, a total of 12,148 hantavirus disease cases were recorded, of which 9714 (approximately 97.41%) were attributed to PUUV infection. In 2019, Europe recorded over 4000 hantavirus cases (0.8 per 100,000), 98% caused by PUUV, with Finland and Germany making up 69% of the total. From 2018 to 2025, Hungary recorded 51 lab-confirmed hantavirus infections, 20 of which were specifically linked to the PUUV. In Finland, between 560 and 3800 cases of NE are reported each year, though the actual number is believed to be nearly six times higher. PUUV is a spherical enveloped pathogen characterized by a segmented negative-sense single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) genome. The PUUV possesses a tripartite genome: the L segment (~ 6.5 kb) encodes a ~ 2156-amino-acid L protein (RNA-dependent RNA polymerase) with replicase, transcriptase, and endonuclease functions; the M segment (~ 3.7 kb) encodes a ~ 1148-amino-acid glycoprotein precursor that is co-translationally cleaved into Gn (70 kDa) and Gc (55 kDa); and the S segment (~ 1.8 kb) encodes a ~ 433-amino-acid nucleocapsid (N) protein. Gc is the protein that mediates fusion by the identification of a peptide of fusion, whereas Gn serves as a folding chaperone for Gc and controls the time of fusion; both are necessary for the virus to adhere as well as enter host cells. Gn and Gc form the principal antigenic surface of PUUV and are major targets of neutralizing antibodies, contributing to protective immunity and vaccine relevance. The N protein plays multiple roles in viral genome transport, replication, and assembly through its interactions with host cellular proteins, while also acting as a highly immunogenic viral component in both humans and animal models. The N protein is highly conserved among orthohantaviruses and elicits a strong early antibody response during acute infection, making it an important target for both diagnostic applications and vaccine development. Various vaccine platforms are available, each possessing distinct advantages and drawbacks. For example, live attenuated vaccines trigger strong, long-lasting immunity but can be risky for immunocompromised individuals due to possible reversion to virulence; inactivated vaccines are safer and more stable, though they usually require multiple doses; subunit vaccines use only key antigens, lowering the chance of side effects, but often need adjuvants and booster shots to achieve durable protection. Moreover, DNA vaccines offer rapid, stable, and cost-effective production with long-lasting immunity, but they often show weak immunogenicity in humans and face delivery challenges. In contrast, the key advantage of mRNA vaccines lies in their rapid design and production, enabling swift responses to emerging infections and pandemic threats without the need to culture live pathogens. In recognition of these advances, the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine honored Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman for their groundbreaking contributions to nucleoside engineering, a key innovation that enabled the successful development of mRNA vaccines against COVID-19. Recent developments in bioinformatics have improved biopharmaceutical design by enabling rapid prediction of protein features, structural modeling, and immunogenicity assessment. These computational approaches accelerate the identification and optimization of therapeutic candidates while reducing time and experimental costs; however, challenges related to prediction accuracy, biological complexity, and the need for experimental validation remain important considerations. Reverse vaccinology (RV) applies bioinformatics and immunoinformatics to screen microbial genomes for conserved, immunogenic epitopes, enabling faster, safer, and cost-effective vaccine development compared to traditional pathogen culturing, a slow and labor-intensive process. Vaccine development against PUUV infection has included inactivated whole-virus vaccines, recombinant subunit vaccines, virus-like particle (VLP)-based approaches, and DNA vaccines. Among these, inactivated and DNA vaccine candidates have demonstrated promising immunogenicity in preclinical studies. Currently, no vaccine has been authorized by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for PUUV infection. Several studies have suggested the potential of multi-epitope vaccine approaches using immunoinformatics-based strategies. Khan et al. developed a multi-epitope vaccine candidate against SARS-CoV-2 by integrating epitope prediction, antigenicity assessment, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and immune response analysis, demonstrating the feasibility of computational vaccine design approaches. Similarly, Peele et al. designed a multi-epitope vaccine construct containing predicted B-cell and T-cell epitopes and evaluated its structural and immunological properties through computational analyses. These studies highlighted the potential of combining multiple immune targets within a single vaccine construct; however, their findings remained primarily dependent on computational predictions and required experimental validation to confirm immunogenicity and protective efficacy. However, despite these advances, several challenges remain in current multi-epitope vaccine development strategies. Computational vaccine designs are dependent on prediction algorithms, reference databases, structural modeling assumptions, and available biological information, which may influence the reliability of predicted vaccine candidates. In addition, variations in epitope selection criteria, antigen conservation analysis, population coverage evaluation, and structural validation approaches can affect the effectiveness of computational vaccine design. Recent studies have emphasized that although immunoinformatics approaches accelerate multi-epitope vaccine development, comprehensive experimental validation remains essential for confirming biological relevance and protective potential. Despite previous vaccine development efforts, including inactivated whole-virus vaccines, recombinant subunit vaccines, virus-like particle (VLP)-based approaches, and DNA vaccine candidates, no PUUV vaccine has currently received regulatory approval. An integrated mRNA multi-epitope vaccine strategy targeting conserved regions of both PUUV glycoproteins (Gn/Gc) and nucleocapsid protein remains insufficiently explored. A comprehensive framework combining conserved antigen identification, multi-epitope vaccine construction, structural evaluation, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and immune response prediction for PUUV has not been extensively investigated. Therefore, this study aimed to design and evaluate the PV-GNProtecta vaccine candidate using an integrated immunoinformatics workflow involving conserved antigen identification, epitope prediction, structural modeling, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and immune response prediction. The findings provide computational insights into the potential characteristics of PV-GNProtecta while recognizing the necessity of experimental validation for future assessment. Materials and methods Acquisition and characterization of viral protein sequences The UniProt protein database (https://www.uniprot.org/; accessed on 15 July 2025) was used for obtaining amino acid sequences of the target proteins from PUUV of G (accession number: P41266) and N (accession numbers: P41270). The G and N proteins were selected due to their key roles in PUUV infection and immune recognition. The G protein mediates viral attachment and entry and is a major target of neutralizing antibodies, whereas the highly conserved N protein contributes to viral replication and induces strong immune responses. Compared with the intracellular RdRp/L protein, G and N provide more suitable targets for antibody and cellular immune responses. A comparative evaluation of these proteins is provided in Supplementary Table S14. Physicochemical and structural characterization of selected proteins The selected PUUV G and N proteins were characterized for signal peptide presence, transmembrane regions, and subcellular localization. Signal peptide prediction was performed using SignalP 6.0 (https://services.healthtech.dtu.dk/services/SignalP-6.0/; accessed on 15 September 2026) with the organism group selected as Eukarya and the default prediction model. Transmembrane topology was predicted using DeepTMHMM version 1.0.57 (accessed on 15 September 2026) using the default settings. Subcellular localization information was obtained from UniProt (https://www.uniprot.org/; accessed on 15 September 2026) based on available curated annotations. Analysis of multiple sequence alignment and evolutionary relationships To support RV analysis, the sequence is encoded using amino acid residue codes and preserved as a FASTA sequence file. The acquired sequences were subsequently utilized for multiple sequence alignment (MSA) through the Clustal Omega platform (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/jdispatcher/msa/clustalo; accessed on 05 August 2025). The Mega X tool (https://www.megasoftware.net/; accessed on 05 August 2025) was employed for phylogenetic analysis on both genomes. Prediction of epitopes for MHC I, MHC II, and linear B-cell interactions The MHC I epitopes from the G and N proteins were found using the Immune Epitope Database (IEDB) (http://tools.iedb.org/mhci/; accessed on 20 August 2025) software, with a percentile rank < 1.00 as the selection criterion. This tool is a sophisticated database comprising information on MHC molecules, T-cell and B-cell epitopes, antibodies, and MHC-binding ligands identified in humans and various animal taxonomic groups, including primates and rodents. A cutoff percentile rank of less than 1.00 was implemented for epitope selection, which suggests that the binding affinity was improved. Lower percentile rank values indicate stronger predicted peptide–MHC binding affinity. The IEDB (http://tools.iedb.org/mhcii/; accessed on 20 August 2025) was applied to forecast the MHC II epitopes inside the designated areas of these proteins, and peptides with percentile ranks < 1.00 were considered potential high-affinity binders and selected for further evaluation. Subsequently, the human allele reference sets were employed to predict CD8 + and CD4 + binding. The ABCpred tool (https://webs.iiitd.edu.in/raghava/abcpred/; accessed on 25 August 2025) was used to estimate the continuous B-cell epitopes of the selected portions of these proteins. This tool provides epitope predictions by analyzing the sequence features of the target antigens. This program uses an affinity scale method based on a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) to predict continuous B-cell epitopes. Additionally, the MHC-II epitopes underwent some additional analyses, including IL-10 (https://webs.iiitd.edu.in/raghava/il10pred/; accessed on 25 September 2026), IFN-gamma (https://webs.iiitd.edu.in/raghava/ifnepitope/predict.php; accessed on 25 September 2026), IL-2 (https://webs.iiitd.edu.in/raghava/il2pred/; accessed on 25 September 2026) and IL-4 (https://webs.iiitd.edu.in/raghava/il4pred/design.php; accessed on 25 September 2026) by using the respective servers. Linear B-cell epitopes were forecasted with ABCpred with a standard window length of 16 amino acids and a score cutoff of 0.51. Antigenicity was evaluated using the VaxiJen v2.0 (https://www.ddg-pharmfac.net/vaxijen/VaxiJen/VaxiJen.html; accessed on 28 August 2025) server under the viral protein model with the default threshold value of 0.4. Peptides with antigenicity scores ≥ 0.4 were considered probable antigens and retained for further analysis, whereas those scoring below this threshold were excluded. The threshold value of 0.4 was selected based on the default classification cutoff recommended for the VaxiJen viral model, which was established through performance evaluation of the prediction system. AllerTOP v2.1 (threshold: 0.5) (https://www.ddg-pharmfac.net/allertop_test/; accessed on 28 August 2025) and ToxinPred (threshold: 0.0) servers (https://webs.iiitd.edu.in/raghava/toxinpred/algo.php; accessed on 28 August 2025) were deployed in order to make predictions on allergenicity and toxicity, respectively. The allergenicity was evaluated utilizing AllerTOP v2.1 with the server's standard ACC/k-NN algorithm configurations. Also, toxicity prediction was performed using the ToxinPred server with the SVM (Swiss-Prot)-based prediction method, applying the default threshold value of 0.0 and a window length of 17 residues. Peptides were classified according to the server-generated SVM prediction score, and sequences predicted as toxic were excluded, whereas non-toxic peptides were retained for further analysis. All settings were preserved according to the server’s default configuration. The selected epitopes were not chosen based only on prediction scores; additional analyses, including antigenicity, safety assessment, sequence conservation, population coverage, and MHC interaction evaluation, were also considered to improve the reliability of epitope selection. full_text_sections.full_text: Design and in silico evaluation of PV-GNProtecta: an mRNA multi-epitope vaccine candidate against Puumala virus using immunoinformatics and structural analysis Puumala virus (PUUV), the principal causative agent of nephropathia epidemica (NE), poses a significant public health threat due to its zoonotic transmission, renal complications, and the lack of an approved vaccine. In this study, an immunoinformatics-driven mRNA multi-epitope vaccine, PV-GNProtecta, was designed using conserved regions of the viral glycoprotein (G) and nucleoprotein (N). Highly antigenic, non-allergenic, and non-toxic T-cell and B-cell epitopes were identified and assembled with appropriate adjuvants to enhance immunogenicity. Population coverage analysis suggested broad HLA responsiveness across diverse populations. The vaccine construct exhibited favorable physicochemical properties, including stability, solubility, and antigenicity. Structural validation predicted high model quality, with 95.5% of residues located in favored Ramachandran regions and an ERRAT score of 91.4. Molecular docking and MM-GBSA analyses predicted favorable computational interactions between PV-GNProtecta and TLR4, while a 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation provided computational insights into the dynamic behavior of the vaccine-TLR4 complex. Codon optimization suggested compatibility of the designed sequence with an Escherichia coli-based expression framework. Immune simulation predicted potential humoral and cellular immune response patterns, including changes in IgG, IFN-γ, and IL-2 levels. The designed mRNA sequence exhibited favorable predicted secondary structural characteristics; however, further experimental evaluation is required to assess translational efficiency and stability. Although this study is limited to computational analyses and requires experimental validation, the findings suggest that PV-GNProtecta may represent a potential candidate for further investigation against PUUV infection. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s44342-026-00081-8. Introduction Nephropathia epidemica (NE) is attributed to Puumala virus (PUUV), a naturally occurring form of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in humans, which is a zoonotic infectious disease and generally considered a mild-to-moderate form of hantavirus infection within the HFRS spectrum. PUUV (Puumala orthohantavirus) is classified within the genus Orthohantavirus, family Hantaviridae, and order Bunyavirales, as defined by current ICTV taxonomy, and it was previously grouped under the family Bunyaviridae prior to taxonomic reclassification. PUUV infection presents with highly variable outcomes, ranging from subclinical cases (70–80%) to severe HFRS, and carries a fatality rate of about 0.1%. PUUV infection commonly presents with sudden fever, headache, back pain, nausea, gastrointestinal symptoms, thrombocytopenia, hematuria, and varying degrees of acute kidney impairment. In some patients, additional manifestations such as blurred vision, dizziness, insomnia, respiratory complications, oliguria, and subsequent polyuria during recovery may also occur. Although PUUV infection is generally considered mild, severe complications can occur in a subset of patients, including acute kidney failure, hypotension, shock, pulmonary edema, Guillain-Barré syndrome, respiratory distress, disseminated intravascular coagulopathy (DIC), myocarditis, encephalitis, pituitary hemorrhage, seizures, and, in rare cases, multiorgan failure or fatal cerebral hemorrhage. The first identification of PUUV occurred in the early 1980s when the virus was isolated from bank voles (Myodes glareolus) in the Puumala region of Finland. Between July 1989 and June 1996, Finland reported 6701 PUUV infection cases confirmed via serological assays, with the highest incidence in the Itä-Savo district and a mortality rate below 0.1%, and later from 1995 to 2008, 22,681 cases were recorded with an average annual incidence of 31 per 100,000 population, resulting in 13 deaths and 52% of patients requiring hospitalization. PUUV accounts for approximately 93% of all notified hantavirus infections in Germany and caused a major outbreak in 2007 in Baden-Württemberg with 1089 reported human cases, while the highest annual number of PUUV infections in Germany was recorded in 2010 since hantavirus surveillance began in 2001. Also in 2007, Sweden’s Västerbotten County experienced a surprisingly severe outbreak of PUUV infection, with NE rates hitting 313 cases per 100,000 residents. Between 2001 and 2017, a total of 12,148 hantavirus disease cases were recorded, of which 9714 (approximately 97.41%) were attributed to PUUV infection. In 2019, Europe recorded over 4000 hantavirus cases (0.8 per 100,000), 98% caused by PUUV, with Finland and Germany making up 69% of the total. From 2018 to 2025, Hungary recorded 51 lab-confirmed hantavirus infections, 20 of which were specifically linked to the PUUV. In Finland, between 560 and 3800 cases of NE are reported each year, though the actual number is believed to be nearly six times higher. PUUV is a spherical enveloped pathogen characterized by a segmented negative-sense single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) genome. The PUUV possesses a tripartite genome: the L segment (~ 6.5 kb) encodes a ~ 2156-amino-acid L protein (RNA-dependent RNA polymerase) with replicase, transcriptase, and endonuclease functions; the M segment (~ 3.7 kb) encodes a ~ 1148-amino-acid glycoprotein precursor that is co-translationally cleaved into Gn (70 kDa) and Gc (55 kDa); and the S segment (~ 1.8 kb) encodes a ~ 433-amino-acid nucleocapsid (N) protein. Gc is the protein that mediates fusion by the identification of a peptide of fusion, whereas Gn serves as a folding chaperone for Gc and controls the time of fusion; both are necessary for the virus to adhere as well as enter host cells. Gn and Gc form the principal antigenic surface of PUUV and are major targets of neutralizing antibodies, contributing to protective immunity and vaccine relevance. The N protein plays multiple roles in viral genome transport, replication, and assembly through its interactions with host cellular proteins, while also acting as a highly immunogenic viral component in both humans and animal models. The N protein is highly conserved among orthohantaviruses and elicits a strong early antibody response during acute infection, making it an important target for both diagnostic applications and vaccine development. Various vaccine platforms are available, each possessing distinct advantages and drawbacks. For example, live attenuated vaccines trigger strong, long-lasting immunity but can be risky for immunocompromised individuals due to possible reversion to virulence; inactivated vaccines are safer and more stable, though they usually require multiple doses; subunit vaccines use only key antigens, lowering the chance of side effects, but often need adjuvants and booster shots to achieve durable protection. Moreover, DNA vaccines offer rapid, stable, and cost-effective production with long-lasting immunity, but they often show weak immunogenicity in humans and face delivery challenges. In contrast, the key advantage of mRNA vaccines lies in their rapid design and production, enabling swift responses to emerging infections and pandemic threats without the need to culture live pathogens. In recognition of these advances, the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine honored Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman for their groundbreaking contributions to nucleoside engineering, a key innovation that enabled the successful development of mRNA vaccines against COVID-19. Recent developments in bioinformatics have improved biopharmaceutical design by enabling rapid prediction of protein features, structural modeling, and immunogenicity assessment. papers.title: Human febrile illness associated with Yanggou tick virus: Clinical characteristics and epidemiological links to rodents.
papers.abstract: Objectives We identified Yanggou tick virus (YGTV), a segmented flavivirus previously unrecognized as a human pathogen, in a patient presenting with fever and headache. This study aims to characterize the epidemiology and clinical manifestations of YGTV infection in patients with fever of unknown origin (FUO). Methods We conducted a surveillance study at the First Hospital of Jilin University (2020-2025) involving 1,011 patients with FUO. Concurrently, ticks and rodents in the vicinity of the patients' residences and workplaces were collected for viral detection. YGTV infection was confirmed via PCR assays. Positive samples were used for viral isolation, genome amplification, and phylogenetic characterization. An Apodemus agrarius challenge model was established to evaluate viral persistence and shedding. Results Of the 30 confirmed cases of YGTV infection, 10 were co-diagnosed with hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS). The patients showed no clear seasonality or geographic bias. Notably, rodent contact (43.3%) was a more frequent risk factor than tick bites (6.7%). While clinical presentations were non-specific, nearly 50% of the patients presented with gastrointestinal and neurological symptoms. YGTV was isolated from patients, ticks, and A. agrarius (the latter often co-infected with Hantaan virus). Animal models confirmed persistent splenic infection and viral shedding via oral and fecal routes. Conclusion Our findings establish YGTV as an underdiagnosed cause of human febrile illness, underscoring the transmission risks posed by tick vectors and rodent reservoirs. These results highlight the urgent need for enhanced clinical surveillance and diagnostic screening among patients presenting with FUO, particularly in regions where the virus is endemic.

analysis_zh.background: YGTV是一种分段的黄病毒,先前未被认定为人类致病菌,在一例发热伴头痛的患者中被发现;本研究旨在阐明其流行病学特征及不明原因发热患者的临床表现。
analysis_zh.methods: 在吉林大学第一医院(2020‐2025)开展的监测研究中,纳入了1,011例不明原因发热(FUO)患者;在患者居住/工作场所附近采集蜱虫和啮齿动物;通过PCR确认YGTV感染,并进行病毒分离、基因组扩增、系统发育分析,以及使用田野鼠(Apodemus agrarius)挑战模型评估病毒的持续感染和排泄情况。

analysis_zh.limitations: 仅有摘要信息可得,限制了对研究设计、统计分析及更广泛推广性的细节描述。

papers.title: Hantavirus in Dentistry: Occupational Exposure Considerations and a Proposed Tiered Infection Prevention and Control Framework-A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Objective The aim of this study is to synthesize evidence on hantavirus transmission and occupational exposure pathways relevant to dentistry, and to propose an evidence-informed tiered infection prevention and control (IPC) framework that distinguishes established from theoretical risk. Material and methods The initial narrative search covered database inception through May 15, 2026 in MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, Google Scholar, and WHO/CDC/ECDC/OSHA sources, followed by a targeted PubMed/MEDLINE and public-health guidance update through August 18, 2026. Approximately 1450 records were identified. After duplicate removal, 1070 records were subjected to title/abstract screening, 215 full-text records were assessed for eligibility, and 45 sources were included in the final synthesis, comprising 34 peer-reviewed publications and 11 gray-literature or public-health guidance sources. Results Environmental exposure to infected-rodent contamination is the established occupational pathway. Limited person-to-person transmission is documented for the Andes virus (ANDV), but no dental transmission has been reported. ANDV RNA and culture-based infectivity have been demonstrated in some oral/respiratory fluids; however, dental-aerosol transmission has not been shown. Dental-specific occupational risk therefore remains unquantified. Conclusions No dental transmission has been documented, and patient-related risk remains uncertain. Standard precautions and rodent control are foundational; suspected or confirmed ANDV warrants transmission-based precautions and airborne precautions for aerosol-generating procedures according to current guidance. The proposed dental tiers are evidence-informed, author-derived, and unvalidated.

papers.title: DNA and mRNA Vaccines Against Hantaviruses: Antigen Design, Delivery Strategies and Translational Progress.
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are members of the Hantaviridae family, which can cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS). At present, no specific antiviral treatment is available for hantavirus infection, while licensed hantavirus vaccines are restricted to a limited number of countries in Asia. This review summarizes recent advances in hantavirus deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines, focusing on antigen design, delivery systems, immunogenicity, safety and translational development. Peer-reviewed studies published primarily within the past 10 years were evaluated together with available hantavirus vaccine trials registered in ClinicalTrials.gov, with emphasis on Hantaan virus (HTNV), Puumala virus (PUUV) and Andes virus (ANDV). DNA vaccine candidates have demonstrated immunogenicity in preclinical and early clinical studies, with an acceptable safety profile. mRNA vaccines represent a newer approach with promising preclinical evidence of humoral and cellular immune responses. However, they have not yet been evaluated clinically. Studies have also reported the potential for varying degrees of cross-protection between hantavirus species, although protection remains limited by antigenic diversity. Overall, current evidence supports further development of nucleic acid-based hantavirus vaccines, particularly multivalent strategies, with emphasis on standardized evaluation and clinical efficacy.

papers.title: Epidemiology and Economic Burden of Puumala Virus Infection in Styria, Austria, 2003 to 2024.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hantavirus infections cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and impose a potential burden on healthcare systems. However, comprehensive economic data remain scarce. We quantified the inpatient economic burden of hospitalized patients with Puumala virus (PUUV) infections in Styria, Austria's primary endemic region, to identify hospitalization costs and early admission predictors of costs. METHODS: This retrospective cost-of-illness study analyzed 1049 serologically confirmed PUUV hospitalizations across 20 public hospitals in Styria, Austria between September 2003 and March 2024. Costs were estimated using the Austrian performance-oriented hospital financing (Leistungsorientierte Krankenanstaltenfinanzierung) diagnosis-related group system, standardized to 2024-equivalent Euros using consumer price index deflation. Admission predictors of cost were assessed using multivariable γ-generalized linear modeling with multiple imputations. Temporal trends in length of stay were analyzed using weighted segmented linear regression. RESULTS: Cumulative inpatient cost was ∼€10.3 million (mean per-case: €9788) for the entire study period of 21 years. Three epidemic years (2012, 2019, and 2021) accounted for 53.6% of cases and over €5.2 million in expenditure, with peak annual costs reaching €1.93 million (0.274% of total Styrian inpatient expenditure) in 2012. Prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT; cost-ratio 1.024 per second, 95% CI 1.019-1.030) and older age (CR 1.004 per year, 95% CI 1.001-1.008) were independent admission-level predictors of higher cost. Median hospital length of stay declined by ∼50% over the study period. CONCLUSIONS: PUUV hospitalizations impose a sharply episodic but recurrent economic burden on regional healthcare systems. Admission aPTT and age independently predicted cost, but clinical outcomes were not modeled and these variables do not constitute a triage tool. Epidemic preparedness strategies are warranted.

papers.title_zh: 2003至2024年奥地利施蒂利亚地区 普马拉病毒 感染的流行病学与经济负担。

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒感染导致肾综合征出血热,并对医疗系统构成潜在负担。
analysis_zh.methods: 回顾性疾病成本研究,涉及1049例血清学确诊的普马拉病毒住院病例,分布于奥地利施蒂利亚州20家公立医院,时间范围为2003年9月至2024年3月,采用奥地利绩效导向医院融资诊断相关分组系统以及多变量γ广义线性模型与多重插补法评估入院成本预测因子。
analysis_zh.results: 21年累计住院费用约为€10.3 百万(平均每例€9788),其中三年疫情高发期(2012、2019、2021)占病例总数的53.6 %并产生>€5.2 百万费用,年度最高费用为€1.93 百万;延长的aPTT(成本比 1.024/秒,95 % CI 1.019–1.030)和较高年龄(CR 1.004/年,95 % CI 1.001–1.008)是独立的高成本预测因子;住院中位时长在研究期间下降约50 %。
analysis_zh.contribution: 普马拉病毒住院对地区医疗系统造成明显的周期性但持续的经济负担;入院时的aPTT和年龄是独立的成本预测因子,为疫情防御策略提供依据。
analysis_zh.limitations: 未对临床结局进行建模,这些变量并不构成分诊工具;仅有摘要数据可用。

papers.title: Seasonal Dynamics, Host Network Structure, and Environmental Drivers of Gamasid Mite Communities on Small Mammals in a Dry-Hot Valley: A Year-Round Monitoring Study.
papers.abstract: Ectoparasitic gamasid mites on small mammals play crucial roles in transmitting zoonotic pathogens like hantaviruses associated with hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS). To elucidate their community, network structure, and seasonal drivers in xeric habitats, a consecutive 12-month localized survey was conducted in Waxi Village, Binchuan County, a dry-hot valley in Yunnan Province, southwest China, from November 2020 to October 2021. From 1329 captured small mammals (18 species, 89.62% rodents), 12,075 gamasid mites belonging to 33 species were identified. The community exhibited overwhelming dominance by the family Laelapidae (Cr = 99.35%) and genus Laelaps (Cr = 97.37%). Laelaps algericus, L. guizhouensis, and L. nuttalli constituted the dominant mite species (cumulative Cr = 88.96%) and formed a tightly correlated core species cluster. Overall infestation prevalence (PM), mean intensity (MI), and mean abundance (MA) were 46.05%, 19.73 mites/host, and 9.09 mites/host, respectively. The bipartite host-gamasid network revealed a significantly nested architecture (NODFobs = 31.16, Z = 14.03, p < 0.001) with high specialization (H2' = 0.599), anchored by dominant hosts (Rattus andamanensis, Apodemus chevrieri, and Mus caroli). α-diversity analysis showed that Margalef richness, Shannon-Wiener index, and Gini-Simpson index peaked in autumn (November), while troughs occurred in mid-spring (April) and mid-autumn (October). Non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS, stress = 0.0048) and PERMANOVA (R2 = 0.074, p = 0.001) confirmed significant seasonal shifts in community composition. Standard redundancy analysis (RDA) suggested temperature as the primary climatic driver (F = 7.205, p = 0.001; total model explanation = 8.2%). However, partial RDA (pRDA) conditioning on host species identity demonstrated that climatic variables directly accounted for only 0.1% of net variance (F = 0.662, p = 0.521). Our findings indicate that gamasid mite community assembly in this dry-hot valley is characterized by strong species dominance and network nestedness and that seasonal fluctuations are consistent with a host-mediated pattern rather than being directly governed by climate.

papers.title_zh: 干热谷地区小型哺乳动物伪螨群落的季节动态、宿主网络结构及环境驱动因素:全年监测研究。

analysis_zh.background: 小型哺乳动物的外寄生伪螨可传播如 汉坦病毒es 之类的动物源性病原体,导致 肾综合征出血热(HFRS)。
analysis_zh.methods: 在中国云南省宾川县瓦溪村开展了为期12个月的连续局部调查(2020年11月–2021年10月),捕获了1,329只小型哺乳动物(18个物种),鉴定出12,075只伪螨(33个物种)。

papers.title: [Nucleoside analogues in etiotropic therapy of hantavirus fevers].
papers.abstract: Hantavirus fevers (HF) are caused by pathogenic orthohantaviruses and are classified into two clinical forms: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), reported in Eurasia, and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), reported in the Americas. HF are characterised by an acute course with predominant involvement of internal organs: HFRS is mainly associated with kidney damage, while HPS is characterised by severe lung injury. Both diseases may also affect the central nervous and endocrine systems. In addition, hantavirus fevers are marked by severe complications during the acute phase and a prolonged recovery period. Currently, there is neither a WHO-approved vaccine nor any effective etiotropic anti-hantavirus therapy. The development of antiviral treatment strategies focuses on preventing orthohantavirus entry into cells or suppressing their intracellular replication. One of the main directions in the search for effective anti-hantavirus therapy is the low-molecular-weight compounds development and testing, many of which have demonstrated pronounced antiviral activity against orthohantaviruses through direct or indirect effects on viral RNA polymerase function. The review shows that new antiviral nucleoside compounds development and study has promising potential, as well as their combined use for effective etiotropic, pathogenetic and symptomatic treatment of hantavirus fevers.

papers.title: Andes virus aboard the MV Hondius: Transnational public health challenges in ocean-going cruise travel
papers.abstract: This article analyzes the cluster of Andes virus infections that occurred aboard the expedition vessel MV Hondius during a transatlantic crossing. Drawing on publicly available information released by the World Health Organization, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, and the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, it examines the key characteristics of this event: probable exposure in a natural reservoir area in South America before embarkation, limited human-to-human transmission in a closed maritime environment, difficulties in early case recognition, and the complexity of international contact tracing. The analysis shows that the vessel itself was not the source of the virus, but rather a setting in which public health risks were amplified due to prolonged cohabitation, limited onboard medical resources, and the cross-border mobility of passengers. Finally, the article highlights the importance of stratified contact management, timely reporting, effective international cooperation, and clear risk communication to avoid both underestimation of the risk and unnecessary public panic.

analysis_zh.methods: 作者对世卫组织、欧洲疾病预防控制中心和美国疾病控制中心公开的资料进行二次分析,重点关注南美储宿区的暴露、有限的人际传播、早期病例识别困难以及国际接触追踪的复杂性。
analysis_zh.results: 该船本身并非 安第斯病毒 的来源;相反,长期同居、船上医疗资源有限以及跨境乘客流动加大了公共卫生风险。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本文强调需要分层接触管理、及时报告、有效的国际合作以及清晰的风险沟通,以防止低估风险和公众恐慌。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供摘要;未在所提供的证据中报告详细方法、定量数据和原始病例信息。

papers.summary_zh: 背景：本文考察了在探险船 MV Hondius 进行跨大西洋航行期间发生的 安第斯病毒 感染集群,强调了跨国公共卫生挑战。 方法：作者对世卫组织、欧洲疾病预防控制中心和美国疾病控制中心公开的资料进行二次分析,重点关注南美储宿区的暴露、有限的人际传播、早期病例识别困难以及国… 结果：该船本身并非 安第斯病毒 的来源;相反,长期同居、船上医疗资源有限以及跨境乘客流动加大了公共卫生风险。 贡献：本文强调需要分层接触管理、及时报告、有效的国际合作以及清晰的风险沟通,以防止低估风险和公众恐慌。 局限：仅提供摘要;未在所提供的证据中报告详细方法、定量数据和原始病例信息。
